Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday that there is no military solution to his country's conflict with the United States, with talks on ending the war apparently at an impasse.
"If our enemies again choose the path of military confrontation, our response will be stronger than before, and we will defend ourselves with even more force," Araghchi said at a gathering of foreign ambassadors. "There is no military solution, nor any solution based on new sanctions."
The US aircraft carrier George H.W. Bush arrived in Thailand's resort island of Phuket on Sunday with about 4,800 personnel aboard for a rest-and-recreation break after six months supporting US operations in the Middle East.
For the last six months, the Nimitz-class aircraft carrier and its strike group supported Operation Epic Fury and the US naval blockade in the US Central Command area of responsibility to secure maritime security and stability in the Middle East, according to the US Navy.
Phuket is the first port call for the George H.W. Bush Carrier Strike Group since departing Norfolk, Virginia, and Mayport, Florida, in March, the US Navy said in a statement.
The Strait of Hormuz will not reopen until seven Iranian conditions set out in a June interim agreement with the US are met, Nournews reported Iran's parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf as saying on Sunday, a few days after Tehran received Washington's reply to its diplomatic proposal.
“The Americans, who say something different in the media, have recently put forward proposals through a mediator. But they must understand that the period of dragging out the process and dictating one-sided demands is over," Ghalibaf was quoted as saying.
"The position of the Islamic Republic of Iran is completely clear and firm, and the Strait of Hormuz will not be opened until our seven conditions, based on the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, are met."

articles.title: 'Very dangerous moment' — Russia sharing jet-powered drone tech with North Korea, Zelensky says
articles.body:
'Very dangerous moment' — Russia sharing jet-powered drone tech with North Korea, Zelensky says
Russia has transferred jet-powered drone technology to North Korea as part of its intensifying defense partnership, President Volodymyr Zelensky said at a press conference on Oct. 4.
Zelensky's comments come a week after he warned that Moscow is preparing to recruit another 10,000 North Korean military personnel to fight alongside Russian troops against Ukraine.
When asked if Russia had also shared its new jet drone technology with Pyongyang, Zelensky's response to journalists was unequivocal: "Yes, of course."
Zelensky outlined Russia and North Korea's history of weapons cooperation throughout the full-scale war, including Pyongyang's supplies of artillery and missiles used to attack Ukraine.
"They're sharing with North Korea all the technologies," Zelensky said. He added that he was not certain if Russia was sharing its ballistic missile supplies as well, but he believed it to be likely.
"I think yes, because North Korea helped them with missiles. It's a very dangerous moment."
The president compared the situation to Russia's cooperation with Iran. Early in the war, Tehran gave Moscow the means to produce its own Shahed attack drones. Years later, when Iran came under attack by the U.S. and Israel, Russia came to its ally's aid with drone supplies, Zelensky said.
Russia has now upgraded its Shahed-type attack drones with high-speed, jet-powered versions that have relentlessly attacked Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities in recent weeks.
Moscow's jet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 kamikaze drones can reach speeds of up to 500 and 600 kilometers per hour, respectively, making them much harder for FPV drones and mobile fire teams to intercept.
The increased use of these weapons in aerial attacks has further exhausted Ukraine's air defenses, already strained by Russia's frequent ballistic missile strikes. In some recent attacks on Kyiv, jet-powered drones have accounted for around two-thirds of all drones launched.
Zelensky said on Sept. 26 that Russia plans to spend $12 billion next year on the production of jet-powered drones and loitering munitions.

articles.title: Germany announces $1.46 billion in aid for Ukraine, including interceptor drones
articles.body:
Germany announces $1.46 billion in aid for Ukraine, including interceptor drones, air defense missiles
Editor's Note: This story has been updated with additional details.
Germany on Oct. 4 announced a new support package worth more than €1.3 billion ($1.46 billion) for Ukraine, including funding for interceptor drones and energy assistance.
The package was announced by President Volodymyr Zelensky and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz at a joint press conference in Kyiv.
Zelensky said the broader value of agreements reached with Germany during the visit exceeded €8.5 billion ($9.57 billion), including a separate agreement aimed at expanding joint efforts to counter drones.
"The total value of today's agreements is more than €8.5 billion ($9.57 billion)," Zelensky said. "A special agreement was signed that creates more opportunities for our joint counter-drone efforts."
Zelensky said the package included weapons needed immediately, support for Ukraine's energy sector, and funding to produce new interceptors specifically designed to counter Russia's jet-powered attack drones.
"These are weapons that will help now, support for our energy sector — this is very important," Zelensky said.
The package includes €1 billion ($1.13 billion) in military aid, including financing the production of interceptor drones capable of countering Russian jet-powered weapons, Merz said.
"This will quickly and noticeably strengthen Ukraine's air defense, and this reinforcement is urgently needed," Merz said.
The defense package also includes "thousands" of missiles for the German-made IRIS-T air defense systems and the delivery of additional IRIS-T fire units.
Additionally, the chancellor announced around €350 million ($394 million) in energy assistance, including support for generators and repairs to infrastructure damaged by Russian attacks.
He added that the energy package was intended to mitigate the impact of Russian attacks on Ukraine's power infrastructure ahead of winter.
Joint weapons production
The European drone manufacturer Quantum Systems will receive financing from Germany to produce tens of thousands of interceptors in Ukraine.
"Ukraine needs interceptor drones at industrial scale," Sven Kruck, Quantum Systems Co-CEO, said in a press release announcing the agreement. "By expanding production in Ukraine, we can respond faster to the immediate threat while building an industrial capability that will also strengthen Germany and its allies."
The joint production program is designed to adapt to Russia's evolving threats, including the increased use of deadly high-speed jet drones in aerial attacks.
Quantum Systems also signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with the Ukrainian defense company Fire Point on Oct. 4. The two companies have agreed to jointly develop new technologies for unmanned systems.
A number of other German and Ukrainian companies also signed MOUs during Merz's visit.
Ukraine's Culver Aerospace signed a letter of intent with the German company Helsing to cooperate on the mass production of long-range strike systems for Ukraine. The Lviv-based Roboneers also signed an MOU with Germany's ARX Robotics on the development of ground drones.
German and Ukrainian companies also reached a framework agreement regarding 25 and 40 mm air defense systems and 155 mm artillery systems.
The announcements build on Germany and Ukraine's expanded joint defense production. In May, Berlin and Kyiv launched "Brave Germany," a joint initiative backed by Ukraine's Brave1 defense-tech platform to support Ukrainian and German defense companies and accelerate development of new military technologies.
The much-needed weapons package comes as Russia continues to terrorize Ukrainian cities and civilian infrastructure with jet-powered attack drones. "Just this week, Russia has used more than 1,900 attack drones, 1,700 aerial bombs, and 25 missiles against Ukraine. More than 800 of the drones were jet-powered," Zelensky said.
Earlier in the day, Merz visited the National Academy of Sciences building in central Kyiv, which was damaged in a Russian drone strike on Sept. 28.
"Mr. Putin, stop this senseless war," Merz said during the visit, according to dpa. "We are ready for talks, we are ready to speak with one another about ending this war. But these barbaric attacks on the civilian population of Ukraine must stop."
Zelensky described air defense as Ukraine's current "number one priority," saying he and Merz had discussed additional measures the two countries could take together.
The new package was announced during Merz's visit to Kyiv on Oct. 4, where he arrived with German Economy Minister Katherina Reiche and executives from the country's defense and energy sectors.

articles.title: Defense Forces Hit Kaluga Radio Tube Plant Producing Components for Kh-101 and Iskander-M
articles.body:
The Defense Forces of Ukraine hit Voskhod-KLRZ, also known as the Kaluga Radio Tube Plant. This electronics manufacturer produces components for Kh-101 and Iskander-K cruise missiles, as well as Iskander-M ballistic missiles.
The OSINT project Supernova+ reported this on the evening of October 3, citing local residents.
Judging by videos published by local residents, cruise missiles or jet-powered drones were used in the strike. A characteristic jet-engine sound can be heard before the explosion.
Meanwhile, the governor claimed that Russian forces had destroyed 13 UAVs over the Kaluga region and Kaluga itself.
The Varta OSINT project reported that the Voskhod JSC, or the Kaluga Radio Tube Plant, specializes in developing and manufacturing high-reliability microelectronics, semiconductor components, specialized materials for the electronics industry, and equipment for testing components.
The plant produces digital integrated circuits, operational amplifiers, transistor arrays, optocouplers, semiconductor lasers and photodiodes. In a 2012 presentation, the company stated that more than 90% of its products were intended for Russia’s defense industry.
According to Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence, Voskhod is involved in producing Kh-101 cruise missiles. The company manufactured OSM140UD17A and UD601A operational amplifiers for the K003 computing unit, as well as 544UD16U3 amplifiers and N590KN13 analog switches for the Monoblock-L unit.
For the 9M727 missile of the Iskander-K system, the plant supplies trunk transmitters for the Zarya-61M onboard computer. It also manufactures converters, operational amplifiers, logic elements, and analog switches for circuit boards of the GIB-123-4 inertial navigation system.
The company is also involved in the production of 9M723 ballistic missiles of the Iskander-M system. According to Ukrainian intelligence, Voskhod manufactures and supplies RUD20 microchips for these missiles.
Another military-related area of the plant’s work is equipment for maintaining armored vehicles. Its catalog includes the UChS-1G system for chemical cleaning of 125mm tank gun barrels and the PPSG-2-2 device for testing generator systems of BMP-2 and BMP-3 infantry fighting vehicles, as well as the starter-generator system of the T-72 tank. The company’s public catalog also offers the PKV-003 device for crimping, or mechanically securing, fuzes screwed into artillery ammunition ranging from 37mm to 152mm in caliber.
Ukraine imposed sanctions on Voskhod under Decree No. 227/2023 dated April 15, 2023, for a period of 10 years. At the same time, the company is not subject to sanctions imposed by the United States, the European Union, or the United Kingdom.
In early September, it was reported that almost half of the 155 companies owned by the Russian Roselectronika industrial holding, which specializes in developing and manufacturing radio-electronic components, remain outside sanctions.

articles.title: Merz makes surprise visit to Kyiv: Germany pledges further aid to Ukraine
articles.body:
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz made a surprise visit to Kyiv on Sunday. Accompanied by Economy Minister Katherina Reiche and representatives of German defence and energy companies, he aims to pledge further military and financial support for Ukraine.
Friedrich Merz arrived in the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, by special train on Sunday morning. The visit had not been publicly announced beforehand. Alongside Merz was Economy Minister Katherina Reiche, as well as around ten representatives of German companies from the defence and energy sectors.
The focus of the trip is further support for Ukraine in its war against Russia. According to German government sources, thousands of interceptor drones are to be delivered to the Ukrainian armed forces in the coming months. The systems are designed to counter Russian jet-powered drones, which are difficult to intercept due to their high speeds.
In addition, joint production of long-range weapons between Germany and Ukraine is to be expanded. Around one billion euros from already approved budget funds is to be made available for this purpose. A further €350 million from Germany is earmarked for the repair and reconstruction of damaged Ukrainian power plants.
Merz: Ukraine needs support now
Upon his arrival, Merz justified his trip by pointing to the current situation in the country. Ukraine needs “all our support for the coming weeks,” the German chancellor said. Referring to the upcoming fifth winter of the war, he pointed to Russian attacks on cities, homes and energy infrastructure.
In Kyiv, Merz was welcomed by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Their talks are expected to focus not only on military support, but also on energy supplies and further cooperation between the two countries.
The trip is taking place under particularly tense security conditions. On Saturday, Russia warned foreign nationals and diplomats against travelling to Kyiv, advising them to leave the city due to the risk of Russian airstrikes.
In the morning, according to Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko, a road on the northern bridge over the Dnipro River was hit by at least one Russian drone.
Speaking to reporters, Merz addressed a message to Russian President Vladimir Putin: “Mr Putin, stop this senseless war! We are ready for talks, we are ready to discuss how to end this war. But these barbaric attacks on Ukraine’s civilian population must stop.”
Merz is increasingly relying on military pressure. Russia only understands the “language of strength”, the chancellor said.
Merz: Expand defence cooperation
In addition to immediate military aid, Merz’s visit also focuses on closer cooperation between the German and Ukrainian defence industries. According to Reuters, the two sides are seeking to advance an agreement on the joint development and production of drones. The focus is on systems designed to counter particularly fast Russian drones.
The German government is increasingly linking military support to closer industrial cooperation between the two countries. The German delegation, which includes representatives from the defence and energy sectors, is therefore also preparing economic agreements and declarations of intent.
For Merz, this is his second visit to Ukraine since taking office as chancellor. Just days after being sworn in, he travelled to Kyiv in May 2025 alongside then-British Prime Minister Keir Starmer, French President Emmanuel Macron and Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk.
With the announced billions in aid and deeper defence cooperation, the German government is signalling its continued support for Ukraine.
Union under pressure: AfD extends lead
For Merz’s CDU/CSU alliance, the latest INSA Sunday poll is a worrying signal: the CDU and CSU fall by another percentage point to 18%, the lowest figure INSA has recorded for the alliance so far.
At the same time, the AfD rises to 30%, reaching a new high. The gap between the two parties has widened to 12 percentage points.
AfD co-leader Alice Weidel commented on the chancellor’s visit to Ukraine on the social media platform X on Sunday.
The SPD and Greens follow at 14% each, while the Left Party stands at 10%. The FDP and BSW are both at 4%, below the 5% threshold.
The poll also paints a poor picture of the federal government overall: the CDU/CSU and SPD together receive just 32%.
At the same time, approval of Chancellor Friedrich Merz has fallen to a new low. Only 15% are satisfied with his performance, while 79% are dissatisfied. Approval of the federal government is even lower, at 14%, with 79% rating its performance negatively.
For the Sunday trend, INSA surveyed 1,202 people between September 28 and October 2. The figures on satisfaction with the chancellor and federal government are based on a separate survey of 1,001 people conducted on October 1 and 2.
Support for Ukraine is eroding
The ARD-Deutschlandtrend poll at the beginning of September already showed a clear east-west divide: in eastern Germany, more than half of respondents believed that German support for Ukraine had gone too far. Against this backdrop, the latest state elections can also be interpreted as reflecting growing scepticism towards Germany’s policy on Russia and Ukraine.
Support for Ukraine remains higher in western Germany and Berlin. But scepticism is also growing nationwide: more than four in ten respondents now say that German support for Ukraine has gone too far. This is the highest level recorded since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022.
The trend is clear: support for Ukraine remains, but approval of Germany’s current aid policy is coming under increasing pressure.

articles.title: 1 killed, 6 injured in Ukraine as another Kyiv bridge comes under Russian attack, Zelenskyy says
articles.body:
Kanyshai Butun
04 October 2026•Update: 04 October 2026
At least one person was killed and six others injured in overnight Russian attacks on Ukraine, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Sunday.
Zelenskyy said a Russian drone again struck the Pivnichnyi Bridge in Kyiv, as key bridges in the capital were targeted for a fourth consecutive day.
He said Russia also struck a medical supply warehouse in Sumy and a communications facility in Dnipro.
Zelenskyy said Russia launched 135 attack drones at Ukraine, more than 50 of them jet-powered, targeting residential buildings and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, Dnipro, Kharkiv, Donetsk and Sumy regions, as well as Zaporizhzhia.
“There are power outages in some communities. Our services are working at the impact sites,” he said.
He said Russia had used more than 1,900 attack drones, 1,700 aerial bombs and 25 missiles against Ukraine this week alone.
“More than 800 of the drones were jet-powered, and Russia must be held accountable for this escalation,” he said.
Zelenskyy also welcomed German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s visit to Kyiv after he arrived Sunday morning, saying Germany had consistently supported efforts to protect Ukrainian lives from Russian strikes.
“We are grateful for all the support, and today we are preparing decisions to give us in Ukraine, and all of Europe, greater capabilities to defend ourselves. There will be important agreements between Ukraine and Germany. Russia must be stopped together,” he said.
Meanwhile, Russia’s Defense Ministry said its forces continued to strike Ukrainian port infrastructure and maritime vessels allegedly supporting Ukrainian troops. It said a dry-cargo vessel carrying military supplies for the Ukrainian armed forces was hit by a drone at sea east of Odesa.
The ministry also said a UAV command post and temporary deployment sites of Ukrainian forces in the Donetsk and Sumy regions came under airstrikes.
It added that Russian air defenses intercepted or destroyed 559 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones over several Russian regions, annexed Crimea, and the Black and Azov seas.

articles.title: “Mr Putin, put an end to this senseless war”: Merz in Kyiv, with €1 billion in military aid
articles.body:
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in Kyiv on an unannounced visit on 4 October and announced more than €1.3 billion ($1.5 billion) in new German support for Ukraine, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said at a joint press conference. Part of the money will fund interceptors against Russia's jet-powered drones, as Russian drones struck Kyiv again during Merz's visit. Merz also pledged to speed up Ukraine's EU accession and announced a Coalition of the Willing meeting in Berlin this winter.
Russia now attacks Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities daily, increasingly with jet-powered drones that outrun the cheap interceptors built for slower Shaheds. That leaves Ukraine dependent on scarce air defense missiles and on partners willing to pay for new weapons fast.
A package aimed at Russia's jet drones
The €1 billion ($1.13 billion) military part of the package includes funding for joint production of interceptor drones against jet-powered drones, Merz said. Recent technological progress means the new interceptors can quickly enter serial production, he added.
"This will quickly and noticeably strengthen Ukraine's air defense," Merz said.
The package also includes long-range weapons, combat drones, and satellite equipment, which Merz said should help Ukraine destroy Russian launchers more effectively. A separate €350 million ($394 million) will go to Ukraine's energy sector before winter, covering generators, transformer substations, and repair kits, Liga reported.
The two countries also signed an agreement on counter-drone cooperation, Merz said. He stressed that the help runs both ways, with German defense companies learning from Ukraine's war experience. The broader deal also covers joint development of weapons with a range of more than 1,000 km, Reuters reported.
Russia’s drones keep targeting the bridges Kyiv can’t easily replace—now the Northern crossing is cratered
Among interceptor drones, the Bars has so far shown the best results, downing up to 30% of its targets, Zelenskyy said. He expects the first results from small missiles designed to counter jet drones in the second half of October.
"We will not be intimidated"
Before the visit, Russia's Foreign Ministry warned foreign nationals and diplomats against staying in Ukraine and threatened new massive strikes on Kyiv. Merz arrived by train with Economy Minister Katherina Reiche and a delegation of German business executives.
"Despite the threats that have reached us from Moscow in recent days, I came today... This shows: we will not let ourselves be intimidated," Merz said.
Merz and Zelenskyy visited the National Academy of Sciences, where a Russian drone killed two people and injured seven on 28 September, the State Emergency Service and the Office of the President said. An air-raid alert sounded while they spoke with rescuers, and emergency service chief Andrii Danyk showed Merz the movement of Russian drones in real time. The same day, a Russian drone hit Kyiv's Northern Bridge again.
"I can only repeat it once again from this point: Mr Putin, put an end to this senseless war," Merz said during the visit. "We are ready for talks, we are ready to discuss bringing this war to an end, but these barbaric attacks on the civilian population of Ukraine must stop," he added, Reuters reported.
NYT: France, Germany and UK build joint format to secure Europe a place in Ukraine peace talks
Zelenskyy called the chancellor's presence despite the alert "a needed and brave signal" from Merz personally and from all of Germany.
EU path and a Berlin meeting
Germany wants to speed up Ukraine's EU accession and is working toward that in Brussels, Merz said. He welcomed Zelenskyy's assurances on rule-of-law and anti-corruption reforms, which he said matter for further financial aid. Together with France and the UK, Germany plans to host a Coalition of the Willing meeting in Berlin this winter to coordinate further support, he added.
The trip was Merz's second to Ukraine as chancellor and his fourth since the full-scale invasion. He arrived just as his standing at home is slipping: the far-right AfD reached 30% for the first time in an INSA poll for Bild, while Merz's CDU/CSU fell to a record low of 18%. Days earlier, Merz had directly accused the AfD of having "Russian backers."

articles.title: Iran warns US: More firepower will not end Mid-East war
articles.body:
Iran warns US: More firepower will not end Mid-East war
- Iran’s top diplomat said there is no military solution to the US war and only negotiations based on justice and fairness can end the conflict.
- The US has rejected Iran’s demands to end sanctions and lift a naval blockade on the Strait of Hormuz, but says it remains open to talks.
- The US has increased military presence in the Middle East, deploying missile batteries and aircraft carriers to counter Iran.
AI generated
TEHRAN – Iran’s top diplomat insisted on Oct 4 that there would be no military solution to the US’ war against Iran, with talks on ending the conflict apparently at an impasse.
A campaign of heavy bombardment failed to bring a decisive close to the war launched by the US and Israel in late February, and Washington in recent weeks has dialled back military operations in favour of economic pressure.
The main point of contention remains Iran’s attempt to blockade the Strait of Hormuz, a vital conduit for Gulf oil and gas where a British maritime agency reported on Oct 4 another tanker struck by an unknown projectile.
“If our enemies again choose the path of military confrontation, our response will be stronger than before and we will defend ourselves with even more force,” Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said at a gathering of foreign ambassadors.
“There is no military solution, nor any solution based on new sanctions,” he said, adding that “only negotiations based on justice and fairness” could end the conflict.
The two sides agreed on a memorandum of understanding in June that spelled out a framework for a permanent resolution, but Iranian attacks on vessels in the Hormuz prompted a return to US military operations.
Iran has sought to impose its control over the vital shipping lane since the start of the war, striking vessels that attempt to transit without its authorisation.
The US has imposed its own counterblockade of Iranian ports, and has also struck vessels it accuses of violating it.
On Oct 4, the British maritime security agency UKMTO said a tanker in the Hormuz “reported being struck by an unknown projectile, causing damage to the engine room”, though the crew were reported safe and no environmental impact was recorded.
The agency did not specify the date of the incident, the vessel’s origin or destination, or whether it was an oil tanker or LNG carrier.
Focused on Hormuz
Iranian and US officials last week held indirect talks on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, with Tehran saying it presented seven conditions for reopening the strait.
Iran has demanded, among other things, a ceasefire across the Middle East, the unfreezing of its assets abroad, the lifting of sanctions on its oil sector and an end to the US naval blockade.
Trump, however, rejected the proposal, while leaving the door open both to further talks or renewed military operations.
Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said on Oct 4 that the US had expressed its views on the proposal and said they were being reviewed.
“The Americans, through intermediaries, have also conveyed their views on this proposal, and these views are currently being examined inside the country through the relevant channels and procedures,” he told reporters, according to state news agency IRNA.
“Whenever the final position of the Islamic Republic of Iran is ready, appropriate steps will be taken accordingly. At the same time, the Islamic Republic of Iran is also preparing itself for any other possible scenario.”
Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei on Oct 4 characterised the latest US counterproposal as being “in line with their previous proposals concerning nuclear issues”.
“We have clearly indicated that we are focusing on the issue of the Strait of Hormuz,” he said, adding that reopening the waterway required “an end to the disruptions to Iranian commercial maritime traffic and the lifting of sanctions”.
The US and Israel have characterised the war as being necessary to prevent Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons – a goal it has long denied pursuing – though the focus soon shifted to reopening the Hormuz after its closure sent shockwaves through world energy markets.
The US has not struck Iran since Sept 1 1, but it has recently pursued a fresh military buildup in the region.
US media outlet Axios reported that Washington has deployed additional Patriot missile batteries to Saudi Arabia and Qatar to help protect key energy facilities from possible Iranian retaliation.
It also reported that the USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier and its strike group were heading to the Middle East, where they could join two other US carrier strike groups already in the region.
Axios reported that top Trump Cabinet members met on Oct 2 to discuss the war in Iran, as well as the conflict in Yemen, where the Tehran-backed Houthis have been fighting government forces and attacking Saudi Arabia. AFP

articles.title: What a US-China thaw could cost India
articles.body:
What a US-China thaw could cost India
When the leaders of the world’s two largest economies meet, the whole world watches the theatrics, the body language and the substance. Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit to the US and summit with President Donald Trump took place against the backdrop of a surge in China’s global trade, while Trump has been struggling with falling approval ratings at home.
The high-stakes summit centred on symbolic gestures, personal rapport, and major economic and technology tensions. It yielded few breakthroughs on structural disputes. The most tangible outcome was an agreement to extend a critical trade war tariff truce by an additional two months, shifting the deadline to mid-January 2027. China’s export boom defied Trump’s tariff campaign.
From a position of strength, Xi was in no rush to make concessions while Trump was constrained by the costly Iran war that was hurting both his popularity and American wallets. The tariffs to address a trade imbalance with China were actually “killing” the US.
View from Delhi
Few nations have been monitoring the proceedings in Washington with greater scrutiny than India, as Xi-Trump discuss AI governance, tariff truces, critical minerals, regional maritime flashpoints, Taiwan and Indo-Pacific security. The outcome could affect New Delhi’s trade ambitions, supply chains, border security, Quad strategy, energy costs and influence.
New Delhi has been closely monitoring shifts in bilateral ties and supply chain vulnerabilities, and wondering about regional security frameworks like the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue (Quad). Indians have been also wondering why they were being singled out for 100% tariff for trading with Russia, while China was being wooed due high US economic dependences. As China has grown in global stature, it was clear that economic and military strength brings prestige and respect.
The largest and oldest democracies, India and the US, were meant to have congruence of interests and common global perceptions. That a day would come so quickly when the US would woo the communist arch rival and competitor from a relative position of weakness, was not anticipated.
At the core of it all, for some time now, India’s calculations have been based on an enduring fear of the emergence of a US-China “G2.” Something that could position India as a “second fiddle.”
The new emerging duopoly could establish a bilateral framework to partition spheres of influence, resolve global disputes, and manage international security above the heads of leading middle powers or an aspiring great power like India. China could get emboldened towards Asian dominance. Early signals were visible during Trump’s second term that Washington preferred a highly transactional foreign policy. Trump’s tariffs were bound to actually give greater leverage to China which monopolizes critical minerals and technologies and has a balance of payments advantage with all.
Despite structural mistrust between the US and China, these baby-steps towards managed coexistence present challenging outcomes for India. On the other hand, a total breakdown of US-China relations would be even worse for New Delhi and the world.
Washington’s policing failures around the world over the decades, and now never-ending Iran war, have lowered America’s global standing and influence. The tariffs have caused a level of distrust in New Delhi. NATO allies and West Asian friends of the US are running helter-skelter looking for alternative security arrangements and umbrellas.
For a long time India was hoping US support for technology and military capability building would allow it to remain a peer to China in Asia. A cosy bilateral understanding between Washington and Beijing could marginalize India’s diplomatic leverage. India also risks diluting regional bargaining power. In fact, US-China competition also indirectly supported India’s “strategic autonomy.”
In the recent past, India was looking for alternative sourcing through what is called the ‘China Plus One’ manufacturing strategy. American industrial giants that have been eager to exit China dependence have been investing billions of dollars into Make-in-India, especially in consumer electronics, pharmaceuticals, automotive parts, and solar equipment. This has helped boost manufacturing’s share of India’s GDP and expand the country’s exports.
But now if Xi and Trump move towards a comprehensive trade deal, securing American industry interests, then the move towards India could slowdown. A transactional Trump has been vocal about India’s protective trade policies and domestic market restrictions. He may now push for opening India’s agriculture and technology sectors to American firms. Global commodity price volatility is also being watched closely by India. A reconciliation between Washington and Beijing could stabilize global demand, and be good for New Delhi.
China controls roughly 70% of global rare-earth element extraction and nearly 85% of refining capacity. Essential for military hardware, electric vehicle batteries, wind turbines, and advanced electronics, they give Beijing significant leverage over Washington. Any US-China understanding on critical minerals will be good for the world and India.
Just days before the bilateral summit, on September 18, Trump signed into law a bill that allows a 100% tariff on top buyers of Russian energy, primarily China and India. Days later, the US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced that Washington and Beijing had extended their Busan Agreement until January 10, 2027, under which the two sides agreed to avoid new tariffs and trade restrictions on each other.
Will India receive a similar concession? For now, it remains exposed to the tariff threat. Does Trump see India as a softer target? While US threatens India and Brazil, it is more considerate towards China because Beijing exercises much more leverage. Peter Navarro, an American economist and Trump’s senior counsellor for trade and manufacturing, at one point called Ukraine ‘Modi’s war’ - because of New Delhi’s oil imports from Russia. Nobody in Trump’s administration has ever tried to call the Ukraine crisis ‘Xi’s war’. Recall that in July 2025, Washington spared China but imposed an additional 25% on India for buying Russian crude. There is thus increased suspicion that India is in the crosshairs while Beijing keeps escaping US scrutiny.
The US has been concerned about AI malpractice by China and has sought structured AI safety dialogues. India, which aims to become a global hub for AI deployment and digital public infrastructure, is monitoring the discussions closely, so that it does not lose the early mover advantage.
India’s Indo-Pacific strategy relies heavily on the Quad alongside the United States, Japan, and Australia. But under Trump 2.0, the grouping has faced growing uncertainty, with the US president clearly favoring bilateral deals over multilateral frameworks. If Washington ends up softening its position on the South China Sea in exchange for economic concessions, it would send a deeply troubling signal — not only to New Delhi, but to the wider world.
As China becomes a peer power with the US, a weakening American position on Taiwan could embolden the People’s Liberation Army (PLA). While India’s immediate focus remains sovereignty over its territory along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) and its influence across South Asia, an emboldened PLA could be a threat for India. It could weaken India’s position on the painstaking negotiations after the 2020 border conflict. Beijing might become less accommodating toward Indian border positions. Conversely a stable China-US relationship could also bring stability in China-India relations, and reduce the trust deficit. India also does not want Chinese or US influence in South Asia as it considers it detrimental to its security.
India hopes that the Xi-Trump discussions bring stability to the global energy trade. Spiking oil prices are already worsening India’s current account deficit and driving domestic inflation.
Reenergized US-China relations could reduce Russia-China dependency on each other. Russia may then edge closer to India.
Long strategic game
The export juggernaut that Trump sought to tame has kept roaring in what economists are increasingly referring to as ‘China Shock 2.0’. China’s global trade surplus is on pace to top $1 trillion for a second straight year. The Trump administration thought they could use massive unilateral pressure to force China to make concessions, but that did not occur.
The US president had hoped to use the pending $14 billion arms package for Taiwan as a “negotiating chip” with Beijing. With Xi clearly in the driver’s seat it will further unnerve US allies in Asia, especially Japan, South Korea, the Philippines, Taiwan, and the Quad partners. Washington’s resolve to defend Taiwan is again in question.
Washington also sees Xi as uniquely able to exert pressure on Iran to negotiate, but Xi has shown little inclination to do so. Beijing is selling billions of dollars’ worth of goods to Iran through sanctions-evasion. Xi had urged the US and Iran to return to negotiations to end the war, but Xi has not publicly commented on Chinese support for Iran. China is moving from indirect influence to signalling readiness for a direct role. Could China become the next mediator in the US-Iran war?
Xi pressed Trump on Taiwan saying he hoped the US would “handle the Taiwan question with prudence.” Meanwhile, Senate Democrats criticized Trump for failing to publicly address China’s military pressure on Taiwan and called for the immediate delivery of approved military aid and arms sales to the island.
In his characteristic way, Trump said America was “very happy” about Xi’s visit, and hoped that China is “very happy also.” Xi said the US-China relationship had developed into a constructive one of “strategic stability on the basis of respect, fairness and reciprocity,” thus positioning Beijing as an equal to the US on the global stage.
“In some ways, the best thing that we accomplished in this visit is to continue the conversation,” US Ambassador to China David Perdue told Fox News. Showmanship of bonhomie and current positive mood in the relationship could be temporary, given disputes over technology controls, rare earth exports, agricultural trade, and over Iran, Russia, and Taiwan.
The US and China remain strategic competitors across trade, technology, security and geopolitics, yet both governments have simultaneously demonstrated an interest in preventing competition from degenerating into confrontation. There was a talk about a possible hotline between the two countries, and some sort of a broad deal for sharing a progress report of sorts. Nothing of that sort happened.
Xi Jinping is playing a long strategic game. Washington continues to be at war and mired in multiple geopolitical and domestic crises. Beijing is quietly consolidating its economy, political control, restructuring its military and expanding its strategic footprint. China does not need to defeat America, it may only need to outlast American attention. “America is very happy about this visit, and I’m sure China is very happy also,” Trump said. Whether India is happy will be dissected in the corridors of power in New Delhi.

articles.title: Medvedev vows Russia will never sacrifice strategic partnership with Iran
articles.body:
Medvedev vows Russia will never sacrifice strategic partnership with Iran
TEHRAN- Former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev has said the aggression against Iran has had serious consequences for the global economy, with people in the United States feeling the impact at home.
Medvedev, deputy chairman of Russia’s Security Council and a former president and prime minister, made the remarks in an interview with IRINN late Saturday.
“Coercion has its limits,” he said. “Moreover, the aggressive attack on Iran has led to very significant changes in the global economy that the United States has been forced to accept.” He added that rising oil and diesel prices had dealt a severe blow to American taxpayers.
Medvedev also warned that the prospect of a nuclear apocalypse was a genuine possibility, describing it as regrettable.
Referring to the actions of the United States and Israel, he said they had destroyed everything and were responsible for the consequences of their own policies.
“They imposed sanctions. They refused to cooperate. Now let them face the consequences,” he said, pointing to high gasoline and fuel prices, shortages of a wide range of essential goods, and high inflation. “They have essentially created these problems for themselves. Let them enjoy it!”
The Russian official stressed that Moscow posed no threat to Europe or the West and had no interests there just maintaining normal relations with European countries, as Russian leaders had repeatedly stated.
He said claims of a Russian threat were being promoted as a pretext to manipulate public opinion, secure parliamentary votes, win elections and obtain more funding for military budgets.
“We are not seeking to put pressure on anyone, nor do we intend to enter into conflict with anyone,” Medvedev said. “We are entirely satisfied with friendly relations with our neighbors, including Iran, but we are not seeking to dominate anyone. We are equal partners with our friends and neighbors.”
He added that Russia wanted nothing more from Western countries than normal dialogue and peaceful cooperation.
“If they want that, we are ready to do it,” he said.
Medvedev praises Iran’s resilience
Recalling the martyrdom of Leader of the Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei and the funeral ceremonies held in his honor, Medvedev said Iran had continued to maintain a normal and full life despite military conflict and profound grief.
“While driving through Tehran, I noticed that despite the dramatic situation, the grief inflicted on the Iranian people and the military events, Iran continues to lead a normal and full life,” he said.
Medvedev said Russian President Vladimir Putin had held Ayatollah Khamenei in high regard and that this was one of the reasons behind his own visit to Iran.
“We will never sacrifice our relations with the Islamic Republic of Iran, no matter what anyone asks of us,” he said. “We are strategic partners, and we will remain so forever.”
The Russian official also said Moscow was interested in a long-term resolution of the situation in Iran and was prepared to offer any mediation services that could help achieve that goal.
He noted that such issues were regularly discussed with Russia’s partners, including Arab countries and the United States, adding that Moscow had made considerable diplomatic efforts in this regard.
Medvedev said the development of economic ties was equally important, pointing to major geopolitical and strategic projects such as the International North–South Transport Corridor.
“The stronger our cooperation becomes, the more active and robust our economic relations will be, including through major geopolitical and geostrategic projects,” he said, adding that economic instruments could be as powerful as conventional weapons.
Regional security is deteriorating
Assessing the security situation in West Asia, Medvedev described it as extremely grave, attributing the deterioration primarily to 'aggression by the United States and Israel.'
“They had been warned that this would dramatically worsen the situation, yet they went ahead with it,” he said.
Medvedev said US officials should learn from the consequences of the conflict and pursue negotiations rather than military confrontation.
“Instead of war and saber-rattling, we should negotiate,” he said. “Otherwise, the world will face economic collapse.”
He added that the US war against Iran had prompted many countries to consider acquiring nuclear weapons.
Iran–Russia cooperation expands
Medvedev highlighted expanding bilateral cooperation between Iran and Russia in defense, advanced technologies, energy and transportation, including the construction of the Bushehr nuclear power plant by Russia’s Rosatom.
He said Russian companies’ investments had helped account for approximately 7 percent of Iran’s total oil production.
He also pointed to the Rasht–Astara railway project, which is being developed through Iranian-Russian cooperation, saying it could significantly transform transportation and economic activity across the region and become a major driver of regional development.
Medvedev said relations between the two countries had reached an “unprecedented level,” with bilateral trade increasing by 20 percent last year.
He noted that 90 percent of trade among Shanghai Cooperation Organization member states was conducted in national currencies, adding that Iran and Russia, both subject to extensive sanctions, needed to develop additional mechanisms for financial cooperation.
 
Iran’s role in the Strait of Hormuz
Addressing Iran’s position in its dealings with the United States and the security of the Strait of Hormuz, Medvedev said Iran played a key role in safeguarding the strategic waterway by virtue of both its geographical position and international law.
He said Iran had so far fulfilled this role effectively.
Russia, he added, was also interested in the normal operation of the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandab Strait but stressed that the security of these waterways should be ensured through genuine agreements rather than coercion or the use of force.

Ukraine’s New FP-9 Ballistic Missile With Moscow in Range to Be Ready This Fall, Zelenskyy Says
Ukraine expects its domestically developed FP-9 ballistic missile, a longer-range weapon that its manufacturer says is capable of reaching Moscow, to be ready this fall, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Reuters on October 3, Zelenskyy said he had personally contacted Ukrainian defense company Fire Point and urged the manufacturer to accelerate work on the FP-9 following the first combat deployment of Ukraine’s shorter-range FP-7 ballistic missile.
“I said to them, where is my FP-9?” Zelenskyy told Reuters. “We need the FP-9. And the FP-9 will be (ready) this autumn, I’m sure.”
The FP-9 is being developed as a significantly longer-range ballistic system than the FP-7. Fire Point has previously said the missile would have sufficient range to reach Moscow from Ukrainian territory.
The missile has a stated range of up to 855 kilometers and is designed to carry a warhead weighing up to 800 kilograms. The ground-launched system is intended to give Ukraine a domestically produced capability for striking targets deep behind Russian lines.
Zelenskyy’s comments came days after Ukraine announced the first combat use of the domestically produced FP-7 tactical ballistic missile. Reuters reported that the FP-7 has a range of approximately 250 kilometers.
The deployment marked another step in Ukraine’s effort to expand its domestic long-range strike capabilities as Kyiv seeks to reduce its dependence on foreign-supplied missile systems.
In the same interview, Zelenskyy told Reuters that Ukraine plans to intensify strikes against Russian oil refineries in response to Moscow’s expanding attacks against Ukrainian energy, transport, and other infrastructure. He said Kyiv would focus on facilities supporting Russia’s war effort rather than indiscriminately targeting civilian infrastructure.
“We have to respond in any way (we can). With their attacks on our energy, we have to respond on their energy. First of all, oil refiners etc: what gives money to them for this war,” Zelenskyy said. “But we will not respond, of course, just like them, on any civilian objects.”
Ukraine has increasingly invested in domestically developed missiles and long-range drones as restrictions, limited inventories, and dependence on foreign partners have constrained the availability of Western long-range weapons.
Earlier, Fire Point CEO and CTO Iryna Terekh said the FP-9 had entered the final stage of development and was expected to be completed by the end of fall 2026. The missile is designed for a range of about 850 kilometers, sufficient to reach Moscow from Ukrainian territory.

articles.title: Germany's Merz arrives in Kyiv to pledge more support
articles.body:
Germany's Merz visits Kyiv amid Russian strikes
Published October 4, 2026last updated October 4, 2026
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, on Sunday and called on Russian President Vladimir Putin to stop his "barbaric attacks" and end what he called a "senseless war."
Speaking alongside Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at the badly damaged building of Ukraine's Academy of Sciences, where at least two people died in a drone strike last week, Merz said:
"We are ready for talks, we are ready to discuss bringing this war to an end, but these barbaric attacks on the civilian population of Ukraine must stop. I can only repeat once again: Mr Putin, put an end to this senseless war."
Merz arrived in Kyiv by train early on Sunday morning, accompanied by German Economy Minister Katherina Reiche and a delegation of leading figures from German business, including executives from Siemens Energy, Hensoldt, Diehl Defense and Quantum Systems.
"If Russia is not stopped, it will turn its war machine against us sooner or later," Merz said upon arrival.
Air raid sirens blared across the Ukrainian capital throughout the morning, as Kyiv's mayor announced one of the city's bridges had been hit by a Russian drone.
Zelenskyy condemned the attacks and said the capital was experiencing a "terrible situation" with "horrific days and nights." He labeled the Russian attackers "absolute barbarians" and said: "It is vital that Ukraine is not left alone in the face of this terror."
Focus on ramping up drone production
Merz pledged further military and energy assistance during his visit, with Zelenskyy announcing a German support package worth more than €1.3 billion ($1.5 billion).
The package includes €1 billion in military aid and €350 million for energy sector repairs ahead of winter.
Zelenskyy said the two countries had reached 15 agreements worth more than €8.5 billion ($9.6 billion), covering defense cooperation, production, procurement and joint projects in Ukraine.
According to German government sources cited by Reuters and the DPA news agency, the planned cooperation includes the development and delivery of thousands of interceptor drones capable of countering the fast, jet-powered drones Russia increasingly deploys against Ukrainian infrastructure.
The plans also envisage expanding production of long-range weapons capable of striking targets more than 1,000 kilometers (620 miles) away.
Merz emphasized that the partnership would also benefit Germany, with companies from both countries developing technology to strengthen their security.
"German and Ukrainian companies are jointly developing technologies that benefit both countries. That makes us safer and stronger," he said.
Russia strikes Kyiv bridge during Merz visit
The visit came just hours after the Russian Foreign Ministry warned foreign diplomats and other visitors to avoid the Ukrainian capital, and military and government buildings in particular.
"The responsibility for any negative consequences lies entirely with those who ignore this warning," read a statement, which claimed that Russian strikes were responses to "terrorist acts by the Ukrainian armed forces against our country's civilian infrastructure."
In recent days, Russia has attacked several bridges across the Dnipro river as well as energy infrastructure, and the city's mayor, Vitali Klitschko, on Friday said that Kyiv was in a "very dramatic situation."
Further strikes followed on Sunday during Merz's visit, with Klitschko confirming that a bridge had been struck.
"Impact on the road surface of the Northern Bridge. Emergency services are heading to the scene," the mayor wrote on the Telegram messaging service.
But the German delegation was not deterred, with Merz saying upon arrival that "Ukraine will need all our support in the coming weeks" as winter approaches and Russian attacks intensify.
"A fifth winter of war is about to begin," he said. "Russia is bombarding cities, apartments and power stations. I will tell President Zelenskyy today: 'You can count on our help.'"
Merz: 'If Germany wavers, Ukraine wavers'
Merz's arrival in Kyiv marks the fourth such visit to Ukraine by a German chancellor since the full-scale Russian invasion began in February 2022.
His predecessor, Olaf Scholz, visited twice during his three-year tenure, while Merz himself first traveled to Kyiv in May 2025 – just four days after taking office. He was accompanied on that occasion by French President Emmanuel Macron, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk and former British Prime Minister Keir Starmer.
Sunday's visit comes just days after Merz had assured Ukraine of Germany's support, despite isolated resistance and criticism at home.
"If we in Germany waver, Europe wavers," he said on Thursday after conferring the international Westphalian Peace Prize upon the NATO military alliance and its secretary general, Mark Rutte. "And if Europe wavers, Ukraine wavers."
Germany remains Ukraine's most important backer, both militarily and financially, but state elections in September saw significant gains for parties at both ends of the political spectrum who are critical of expenditure on Ukraine: the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and the socialist Left Party in Berlin.
In his speech on Thursday, Merz called out in particular "the AfD and their Russian backers" and promised Ukraine that Germany would not be divided.
Edited by: Zac Crellin, Natalie Muller

articles.title: Germany Pledges €1.3B Defense Package During Merz Kyiv Visit
articles.body:
Germany has committed a comprehensive military and energy assistance package valued at more than €1.3 billion ($1.5 billion) to Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelensky and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz announced in Kyiv on Sunday, Oct. 4.
According to Ukrinform, the newly allocated assistance package comprises roughly €1 billion ($1.13 billion) in military aid focused on air defense, long-range strike capabilities, combat drones, and satellite communications, alongside approximately €350 million ($396 million) to reinforce Ukrainian power substations and emergency generation ahead of winter.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Speaking during a joint press briefing in the capital, Zelensky stressed that the agreements combine emergency battlefield deliveries with sustainable industrial integration.
“There is a new support package for Ukraine – a comprehensive package of more than €1.3 billion,” Zelensky stated. “This is weapons that will help right now, as well as support for our energy sector ahead of winter – an important energy package. Naturally, we discussed the need for air defense, which is crucial at this time.”
In parallel with the emergency assistance, the two governments and corporate partners concluded 15 bilateral agreements and industrial documents valued at more than €8.5 billion ($9.6 billion), focusing on long-term arms manufacturing, joint defense ventures on Ukrainian soil, and direct state orders for German industrial manufacturers.
No EU Embassies Leaving Kyiv Despite Russian Threats, Envoy Says
“To date, we have 15 agreements and documents, and most of them concern security cooperation, manufacturing, corresponding procurement, our orders for German industry, and joint projects in Ukraine,” Zelensky said.
“The total weight of today’s agreements is more than €8.5 billion.”
Military breakdown, long-range systems, and winter energy aid
Details outlined by Chancellor Merz during the briefing confirmed that the €1 billion ($1.13 billion) military component prioritizes long-range standoff capabilities and advanced communications to allow Ukrainian forces to target Russian launch installations directly.
“We are launching another military support package worth around one billion euros,” Merz said, noting that Berlin will supply long-range strike weapons, combat drones, and satellite technologies.
“Regarding the details of the military support, I ask for understanding that we do not wish to disclose them in detail.”
Merz emphasized that German military assistance is concentrating on two foundational capabilities: expanding layered air defense and reinforcing space-based satellite communications to ensure Ukrainian units receive real-time operational data.
The chancellor added that German funding is accelerating serial assembly lines for newly developed interceptors engineered to neutralize jet-powered strike drones following recent technological breakthroughs.
Addressing the civilian heating sector, Merz announced approximately €350 million ($396 million) in targeted energy assistance to procure mobile generators, repair damaged electrical substations, and restore transmission infrastructure battered by Russian aerial strikes.
“We are facing what may be a very difficult winter. Moscow is deliberately targeting energy supply infrastructure – thermal power plants, substations, fuel stations, and railway infrastructure,” Merz said.
“The goal is entirely obvious: to break the morale of Ukrainians. Despite the attack that occurred this morning, I see here a determined people and a determined government.”
Industrial ventures and Berlin winter summit
A core component of the newly finalized accords is a dedicated bilateral agreement on joint counter-drone operations, established to counter Russia’s accelerating use of turbojet-powered loitering munitions against Ukrainian urban centers and power generation facilities.
The agreement aligns with Chancellor Merz’s pledge, announced upon his arrival in the capital, that Berlin intends to ensure the expedited transfer of 1,000 newly developed interceptor systems designed specifically to defeat turbojet-powered Shahed drones directly from German production lines.
Merz traveled to Kyiv accompanied by German Minister for Economic Affairs Katharina Reiche alongside a 10-member delegation of chief executives and senior managers representing Germany’s defense and energy industries.
The corporate representatives conducted working sessions with Ukrainian defense officials to advance collaborative assembly lines, technology transfers, and resilient industrial supply chains.
The industrial focus comes as German defense planners and corporate partners seek to deploy lower-cost interceptors capable of neutralizing fast-moving strike drones without depleting high-end surface-to-air missile stockpiles such as the IRIS-T or Patriot.
Looking ahead to multilateral diplomatic coordination, Merz announced that Germany intends to convene a high-level summit in Berlin this winter alongside France and the UK.
“Together with France and Great Britain, we want to hold a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing in Berlin this winter, particularly to coordinate further assistance,” Merz confirmed, though specific calendar dates and formal agendas remain under development.
Academy of Sciences visit
Following their formal talks, Zelensky and Merz traveled together to inspect the site of a recent Russian drone strike on the National Academy of Sciences in central Kyiv.
The strike on the academic institution killed two people and injured seven others, causing severe structural damage to the historic scientific complex.
Zelensky stated that video records confirmed the facility was deliberately targeted by Russian loitering munitions, characterizing the strike as an intentional effort to destroy Ukrainian scientific infrastructure.
The joint inspection took place against the backdrop of recurrent air raid sirens and ongoing drone strikes across the capital on Sunday morning, which included a repeat strike that damaged the road deck of Kyiv’s North Bridge.
Zelensky commended the German chancellor for maintaining his itinerary and visiting the damaged research complex despite operational security warnings, describing the gesture as an important signal of personal and national solidarity from Berlin.
Merz’s visit follows statements delivered in Berlin on Sept. 29, in which the German leader identified territorial air defense as Ukraine’s “weakest point” ahead of the winter heating season, confirming that Germany is coordinating with EU partners to finalize additional military aid packages ahead of the European Council summit in Brussels on Oct. 15–16.

articles.body:
From a drone-downing pastry chef to the company commander who carried a wounded soldier for miles on foot: 10 stories of Ukraine's defenders
2026 has been a year of victories great and small for the Ukrainian military, and the whole country has celebrated along with them.
Nazar Daletskyi, a serviceman believed to have been killed three years ago – a funeral had even been held for him – came home alive from captivity.
Vladyslav Polskyi, a company commander in the 475th Assault Regiment (Code 9.2), single-handedly evacuated two wounded soldiers in a civilian pickup truck as Russian drones circled overhead.
The National Guard awarded the title of Hero of Ukraine to a woman for the first time – machine gunner Oleksandra Davydenko.
Ukraine's defence forces in the south reclaimed up to 435 sq km of territory. The 3rd Army Corps stunned the public with the successful Operation Vivaldi counteroffensive in Donetsk Oblast.
Ahead of Defenders' Day, Ukrainska Pravda.Zhyttia (Life) looks back to 10 of this year's most interesting stories about our defenders. Read them all – you won't regret it!
"Four of them couldn't walk": how a Special Operations Forces company commander evacuated a wounded soldier on foot, then went back for his comrade's body
"Eighteen", a company commander in the Special Operations Forces (SOF), would normally have been expected to coordinate the evacuation from the command post. But when four of his soldiers were no longer able to walk independently after a battle and an encounter with an improvised explosive device, he went into the area himself.
"The guys all had leg wounds. There were two uninjured operators left in the group, plus one medic.
That was when I realised I had to go into the area and get my people out. Nobody could have imagined that out of a group of eight we'd end up with four seriously wounded men and one slightly wounded. Four of them couldn't walk," Eighteen recalls.
It took 15 hours to carry the most seriously wounded soldier, Malyi (Little One), to the medics. The young man had severe injuries to his arm and abdomen and a ruptured liver.
"There were moments when he couldn't take it any more and lost heart. He'd say: 'I don't want to. You don't need to carry me anywhere.' But painkillers make all the difference. Obviously he was in a lot of pain. But he did well and held on," Eighteen says.
As soon as Malyi had been handed over to the doctors, Eighteen went back for the body of his fallen comrade, Sava. The rescue operation took five days in all, and the soldiers covered more than 50 km. All but Sava survived.
This remarkable operation proved once again that even in the era of ground robots, those who operate on their own two feet still have the decisive say in battle.
"I thought about tightening the tourniquets and bleeding to death so I wouldn't suffer": how a badly wounded infantryman hunted by six drones was rescued
Herodotus is a private first class in the 3rd Mountain Assault Battalion of the 128th Separate Mountain Assault Brigade. After 18 months fighting in an assault unit, he miraculously survived being hunted down by six Russian drones.
Herodotus was alone in a wooded area. He had already lost a foot, and as he was being evacuated, a Russian drone destroyed the ground robot and mangled his other leg.
He crawled, hid from FPV drones, and even played "cat and mouse" with one of them around a dugout, moving in such a way as to stay out of the Russians' line of sight. His comrades watched him from a drone throughout, dropping water, painkillers and food and trying to find a way to get him out.
Eventually three soldiers came to retrieve him and carried him for about 2.5 km. Herodotus lost both legs, but he survived. He says that in his darkest moments he remembered that he had promised his family he would return.
"There, look at what I've got now instead of legs. Ta-da! What am I supposed to do now – cry? It's already happened... I'm alive, so everything should be all right. Life can be a complete pile of shit sometimes, but we'll get through it," he says cheerily.
"We accepted that we were going to die": the military anaesthesiologist who volunteered to go to the besieged Azovstal steelworks
In spring 2022, military anaesthetist Oleksandr Demchenko volunteered to fly to the besieged Azovstal steelworks in Mariupol by helicopter. He realised that it could be a one-way trip. He later learned that the helicopter was shot down on its return journey.
At Azovstal, Oleksandr operated on wounded soldiers in an underground hospital, in cold and damp conditions and with a dwindling supply of medicines: even amputations had to be performed under local anaesthetic.
After one airstrike, five floors of the building above the medics collapsed while hundreds of people were inside.
"We all accepted that we were going to die there, because, essentially, there were no other options," Oleksandr recalls. But he was lucky – he made it out of there.
He survived Azovstal, Russian captivity and the Olenivka prison camp. When he returned home, he went back to medicine.
"I returned to the profession because I love it. I genuinely love my work," he admits.
"I'd serve for another six years, as long as my son never sees all this": the nurse who swapped her uniform for combat fatigues
Before joining the Armed Forces of Ukraine, Tamila had worked as a nurse at a district hospital for 15 years. Then she swapped her uniform for combat fatigues, eventually becoming head of the medical station of the 3rd Mountain Assault Battalion of the 128th Separate Mountain Assault Brigade.
In autumn 2022, when the brigade was conducting a counteroffensive in Kherson Oblast, Tamila was constantly going out to evacuate the wounded.
"I provided first aid in the vehicle. I had to stop the bleeding from severed arms and legs, apply tourniquets and administer painkillers. The brigade was carrying out assault operations, and guys were dying both on the battlefield and in front of me," she recalls.
Once, two years later, she happened to meet a soldier whom she had once evacuated with a severed arm. He recognised her first: "You were the one who evacuated me back then. Thank you."
Tamila's first contract ended long ago and she could have left the military, but she stayed. She still goes out on evacuations sometimes, even though her current position does not require her to.
She says she is ready to serve for as long as necessary, as long as her 16-year-old son never has to follow in her footsteps.
"I've been in the Armed Forces of Ukraine for six years now, and they haven't been easy years for me – they've been really hard. Because war is the worst nightmare there can be. But I'm ready to serve for another six years, as long as my son never sees all this, as long as he never has to fight," Tamila admits.
"Several times we had enemy infantry jumping into our trenches": the company commander who spent 343 consecutive days on the front line
Three hundred and forty-three days is enough time to celebrate Christmas, New Year and Easter. But for company commander Oleksii, aka Botanik (Nerd), it was the length of time he spent at positions on the Orikhiv front without rotation.
About half of the soldiers in Botanik's company are over 50, and many suffer from chronic health problems. This makes normal rotations almost impossible, so they have to remain on the line of contact for long periods.
Oleksii's longest combat deployment took place in June 2025. The Russians would attack the Ukrainian positions using infantry fighting vehicles, motorcycles and quad bikes and on foot. When they managed to reach the trenches, machine gunners and drone operators would join the fighting. Evacuation crews collected the wounded under fire.
"I tried to make the fighters' time at the combat positions as bearable as possible. I made sure everyone had a chance to talk to their families every day – that helps a lot," the company commander says.
Oleksii finally left the line of contact on 8 March 2026 and immediately went on leave to celebrate his daughter's 10th birthday. Then it was back to the front line.
"I see my primary role as a commander as minimising personnel losses – ideally ensuring there are none at all," he says.
Pastry chef by day, air defence operator by night: the woman from Bucha shooting down Russian drones
Liudmyla, from Bucha, isn't your typical volunteer. By day she makes exquisite cakes and pastries, but after dark, she protects the skies over Kyiv Oblast.
It all began in 2024, when an acquaintance told Liudmyla about the Bucha Witches – a women's unit of mobile air-defence fire groups established as part of the Bucha Volunteer Formation of the Territorial Community. Liudmyla couldn't stand idly by.
The first time she shot down a Russian Shahed drone, the adrenaline rush was overwhelming. Two years ago she knew almost nothing about the military – now she commands a mobile fire group.
Liudmyla does all this as a volunteer and receives no pay. After a night shift, she returns home, puts down her weapon, and gets back to making cakes.
"It can be difficult at times – exhausting night shifts and winter cold when your hands quite literally freeze to the machine gun – but I love this work. Now I see safety in a completely different way and always silently thank those who protect my sleep when I am off duty," the defender says.
"It was eating away at me that my country was at war while I was here": the Mariupol surgeon who returned from abroad to serve in the army
In March 2022, urological surgeon Dmytro Hetmanov was operating on wounded civilians in besieged Mariupol. The hardest moment came when a father carried in his wounded teenage son. The injury looked minor from the outside, but the boy's heart and blood vessels had been virtually torn apart. The boy could not be saved.
On 16 March, Dmytro decided to try to escape the city with his parents and neighbours. On the way, he saw the bombed-out Drama Theatre still smouldering. It took him a long time to get through the Russian checkpoints.
Two years later, Dmytro was working as a surgeon at the University Hospital in Katowice, Poland. He had a job and his life was gradually getting back on track, but thoughts of his homeland never left him.
"It was eating away at me that my country was at war while I was here. Some of my friends had joined the Armed Forces, while I was sitting here enjoying life," he admitted.
Dmytro resigned and left Poland to return to Ukraine. He completed basic military training, signed a contract and joined the Unmanned Systems Forces. Six months later, he realised that he was missing surgery.
Now Dmytro is serving as a surgeon once again, this time with the 4th Medical Battalion of the 3rd Army Corps. He deals with combat injuries, assists with amputations, and has even tried his hand at neurosurgery for the first time.
Although Dmytro's daughter lives in the United States and rarely sees her dad, he does not regret his decision to join the military.
"They actually listed me among the dead": Azov fighter Web on the Olenivka terrorist attack and rehabilitation after three years in captivity
Dmytro "Web" Tishchenko was listed among the dead after the Russian terrorist attack on the Olenivka prison camp. When he came to, he was lying in a pile of metal and concrete, with a punctured lung and a bleeding arm. He crawled out of the destroyed barracks by himself.
"We asked the Russians for at least some medical supplies, but all they brought us was a bag of army sheets. We tore the fabric into pieces and used them to dress our wounds," the Azov fighter recalls.
When he was finally taken to hospital, one of the Russians was surprised to hear his name called out: "You're alive? I'd already got a body bag ready for you."
Web was only 21 at the time of the terrorist attack on Olenivka. He became a soldier at 18, took part in the defence of Mariupol, was wounded in the leg, made it to Azovstal, and from there he was taken into Russian captivity.
Dmytro spent another two months in hospital after the attack, and then he was moved from one penal colony to another. He had to endure torture, cold, hunger, and being made to stand for hours on end.
Because of a shrapnel wound, his leg became so badly infected that the wound simply opened up. In order to be admitted to hospital and avoid losing the limb, he had to pretend to faint.
Dmytro spent almost three years in captivity. In April 2025, he was suddenly taken out of his cell, given clean clothes and driven to an unknown destination. It was a prisoner swap. Web came home on the eve of Easter – exactly when he had dreamed of returning.
Now Web is undergoing treatment for his injuries and the effects of captivity, while also helping other young soldiers who have returned from Russian captivity.
"Sometimes I forget I'm missing a leg": two Khartiia infantrymen who've returned to service after suffering severe injuries
Assault trooper "Bilyi" stepped on a mine 15-20 metres from his position. He applied a tourniquet himself and waited to be evacuated, but the team that set off to retrieve him was attacked by a drone. When dawn broke, he realised that help might not come in time, so he started crawling on his own.
Bilyi crawled for nearly a whole day before two reconnaissance soldiers found him. By then the tourniquet had been on his leg for about two days. Bilyi had realised immediately after the explosion that his leg would have to be amputated.
"Terry" went through a similar ordeal. During his third combat deployment, he stepped on a petal mine hidden in the grass.
"It didn't hurt, I didn't lose consciousness. I opened my eyes and saw these toes lying around. Only the heel was left. I thought, 'That's it. I've had my run,'" Terry recalls.
It took 25 hours to evacuate him. Along the way, the wounded man and the soldiers carrying him were pursued by Russian FPV drones. One drone missed them, but another exploded near the group, injuring all three of the soldiers who were carrying Terry. Despite their own injuries, however, they managed to carry him to shelter.
Both Terry and Bilyi had their legs amputated. Months of surgery, rehabilitation and prosthetic fittings lay ahead of them. Terry recalls that after receiving a temporary prosthesis, he started walking the very next day and soon left his crutches behind. Bilyi was also quick to learn how to use his prosthesis.
"After they cut off my leg, there were moments when I felt a bit down. Then I'd lie there and think: it's all good. I'm alive, I can eat and get around on my own, go to the toilet and have a shower – I can do all of that," Terry says.
Bilyi is equally convinced: "Life goes on. The main thing is that I'm alive."
Their service didn't end there. Less than a year after being wounded, Bilyi got a call from the company's senior sergeant, who offered him a new position. On 12 May, he rejoined the Khartiia Brigade. Terry later joined him.
The two former infantrymen began learning an entirely different role – they became ISTAR dispatchers at a command and observation post. Instead of going out on combat missions, they now monitor the battlefield through screens, work with reconnaissance personnel and drone operators, and pass on information about targets.
"If I sat at home, what would I do? At least this way I can help out here," Bilyi says.
For now, the Khartiia soldiers have no plans to return to civilian life.
Olena Barsukova
