articles.title: US remains 'hell-bent' on preventing Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons, says Hegseth
articles.body:
US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth warned Iran that US President Donald Trump remains determined to prevent it from acquiring nuclear weapons, cautioning that Tehran must choose between relinquishing its nuclear ambitions and facing further American action.
Speaking to reporters on Saturday, Hegseth also declined to confirm whether the United States intends to deploy a third aircraft carrier to the region, saying his responsibility is to ensure that Trump retains the widest possible range of military options.
Asked directly whether three aircraft carriers would be deployed, Hegseth replied: “It’s a fair question, but I will never answer it.”
“I’d say maximizing the decision space for the commander in chief at any point is my job, while also recognizing the way we balance global demands as a force with global responsibilities,” he explained.
“So the president’s going to have options. Let’s put it that way, and I’ll leave it there.”
‘Iran will never, ever, ever have a nuclear weapon’
Hegseth delivered his strongest warning when asked to clarify the administration’s message to Tehran.
“Well, the message is very simple: Iran will never, ever, ever have a nuclear weapon,” he said.
“President Trump is hell-bent and determined to ensure that they do not. They will not. If they want to blink and think that he doesn’t mean it, it would be to their detriment.”
He added that Iran had reached a decision point.
“So now’s a moment where they can decide to give it up the way that they should, without any leverage that they have, or it may have to happen the hard way.”
Earlier in the exchange, Hegseth was asked whether he expected military operations to conclude before the end of the year. He declined to commit to a timetable, deferring the decision to Trump.
He nevertheless contrasted the administration’s approach with previous American military campaigns that, he said, had continued for years or decades without clearly defined objectives or an identifiable end state.
“As we’ve stated from the beginning, Iran will never have a nuclear bomb. Full stop. That is a vital national interest of the United States of America,” Hegseth said, citing Operation Midnight Hammer and Operation Epic Fury.
He stressed that Trump would not allow operations to continue unnecessarily, arguing that the administration understands its mission and has the capabilities required to accomplish it.
Hegseth acknowledges Iranian efforts to rebuild missile capabilities
Asked whether Washington had evidence that Iran was attempting to reconstitute its missile capabilities and launchers, Hegseth said the United States was monitoring developments in real time.
He acknowledged that Tehran would attempt to rebuild its military infrastructure but maintained that the damage inflicted during Operation Epic Fury had severely complicated those efforts.
“Think of it this way, their Raytheons, their Boeings, their Lockheeds, their Northrop Grummans are what was destroyed in Epic Fury,” he said, referring to the Iranian equivalents of major American defense manufacturers.
“So they’re going to attempt to reconstitute, and they’re a terror state. So they’re going to always attempt to reconstitute, but when you’ve been so destroyed and degraded the way that they have, it’s a very slow process, a very frustrating process, and we see that, and we understand that.”
Hegseth argued that the extent of the damage to Iran’s defense industrial base, economy, and ability to rebuild would continue to constrain Tehran’s military options.
‘They don’t control the Strait of Hormuz, we do’
The defense secretary also emphasized American control over the Strait of Hormuz, describing the US blockade as a central component of Washington’s pressure campaign against Iran.
“Iran wants to play games with things like the Strait of Hormuz. They don’t control it. We do,” Hegseth said.
“Our blockade has been ironclad, and we’re running almost at pre-war levels every single night through that,” he added, referring to maritime throughput.
Hegseth asserted that Iran’s naval and air capabilities had been so extensively degraded that it could no longer effectively challenge American dominance over the strategic waterway.
“It’s pretty tough for them to control the Strait of Hormuz when they don’t have a navy. They don’t have fast boats, and they’ve got no air force,” he said.
“And then we’ve done such incredible damage to their ability to see and sense the Strait of Hormuz. We control it. We dominate it in both an asymmetric and a conventional sense.”
He added that Washington was capable of maintaining the blockade for as long as necessary and adapting its implementation according to operational requirements.
“The longer we hold the blockade, and we can hold it as long as we need to. Trust me, we can adapt that as necessary,” he said, arguing that the pressure would further restrict Tehran’s remaining options.
Asked whether the conflict could ultimately have a military solution, Hegseth said it could be resolved in multiple ways and maintained that Trump had repeatedly offered Iran an opportunity to reach an agreement through negotiations.
“The president has given Iran every opportunity to do it at the table,” he said.
However, he reiterated that the combination of American military strikes and the continuing blockade had left Washington in a strong position.
“Iran ought to make the right choice. If they don’t, the president’s going to have all the options he needs on the table,” Hegseth concluded.

articles.title: Russia Launched 1,900 Drones and 25 Missiles This Week, Zelensky Says
articles.body:
Russian forces launched more than 1,900 strike drones, 1,700 guided aerial bombs, and 25 missiles of various types against Ukraine over the past week, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced on Sunday, Oct. 4.
Writing on Telegram, he reported that over 800 of the unmanned aerial vehicles deployed in the weekly barrage were high-speed, turbojet-powered variants, which travel at higher velocities and altitudes that complicate interception by ground-based mobile air defense units.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The weekly tally followed an overnight bombardment into Sunday morning during which Russian forces launched 135 strike drones across Ukrainian territory, including more than 50 jet-powered models.
Incoming munitions targeted regions including Kyiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Kharkiv, Donetsk, Sumy, and Zaporizhzhia, damaging residential buildings, utility networks, and municipal life-support systems, triggering localized power outages across several communities.
Zelensky confirmed that overnight drone strikes in the northern city of Sumy struck a commercial pharmaceutical storage depot, killing one person. In Dnipro, a Russian strike hit a communications enterprise, injuring at least six people, while a follow-on drone hit the North Bridge in Kyiv.
“It is vital that Ukraine does not stand alone against this terror,” Zelensky stated, emphasizing that international partners must respond to Moscow’s expanding reliance on turbojet loitering munitions.
UN: Ukraine Civilian Casualties Surge 55% in 2026
Capital bridge strikes and transit disruption
The Sunday morning strike on Kyiv’s North Bridge marks the second consecutive aerial attack targeting the strategic river crossing within a 24-hour window, compounding logistical strain across the capital.
Emergency services and municipal transit engineers were dispatched to the bridge after incoming fire blasted a detonation crater into the road deck. Municipal authorities are assessing the physical destruction to determine whether vehicular crossings between the eastern and western districts of the city must face further transit restrictions.
The follow-up attack follows a direct hit on the morning of Saturday, when a Russian turbojet loitering munition struck the North Bridge, tearing up road surface asphalt and severing overhead electrical contact cables that power municipal trolleybuses. 
Klitschko confirmed that two civilians sustained injuries in Saturday’s bridge strike, with one victim treated at the scene and a second hospitalized.
The consecutive hits on the North Bridge follow the complete closure of the South Bridge to vehicular traffic on Friday after repeated drone impacts damaged roadway sections, bridge piers, and structural barriers shielding the Green Line metro crossing.
Сounter-drone interceptors
The surge in weekly bombardments coincides with high-level bilateral defense consultations in the capital following the unannounced arrival in Kyiv of German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
Leading a government and industrial delegation that includes German Minister for Economic Affairs Katharina Reiche and 10 defense and energy corporate executives, Merz arrived on Sunday to formally guarantee expedited military deliveries, including 1,000 newly developed interceptor systems designed specifically to defeat high-speed, turbojet-powered Shahed drones.
Welcoming the German chancellor’s visit, Zelensky commended Berlin’s consistent defense leadership and confirmed that bilateral teams are preparing joint defense agreements to bolster Ukraine’s and Europe’s layered air defense architectures.
“Germany consistently demonstrates leadership in protecting the lives of Ukrainians from Russian strikes,” Zelensky said. “Today we are preparing decisions so that we in Ukraine and throughout Europe have more opportunities to defend ourselves. There will be important agreements between Ukraine and Germany.”

articles.title: Zelenskyy vows to target Russian refineries in response to Moscow's 'new doctrine' on strikes
articles.body:
Ukraine will double down on attacking Russian oil refineries in response to a new policy of air strikes by Moscow designed to force people to abandon Kiev and other cities, but will not target civilians, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said.
Ukraine's intelligence services has obtained documents showing that Russian leader Vladimir Putin had issued a "new doctrine" of military attacks on a much broader range of civilian targets ahead of this winter, Zelenskyy claimed on Saturday.
"We saw documents and we know that they allow them to attack infrastructure, logistics, and especially to attack in the cities, in the villages, everywhere, roads, schools, hospitals," Zelenskyy told Reuters in an interview.
"To pressure people to leave the capital, leave different cities: this is the goal of the operation."
Driving the shift in policy, Zelenskyy said, was Putin's desire to appear strong at a time when his military was losing ground in a key frontline region and sustaining higher levels of casualties.
The Kremlin was not available to comment.
Russia urges foreigners to leave Kiev
But in a statement urging foreign nationals to leave Kiev, the Russian Foreign Ministry said Moscow would continue to systematically hit targets in what it said were retaliatory strikes for Ukrainian attacks on Russia in recent months.
Both sides deny deliberately targeting civilians.
Zelenskyy said a successful Ukrainian counteroffensive, code-named "Vivaldi", had recaptured around 140 sq km of Ukraine's eastern Donbas region and was still ongoing.
Russia has said it must control Donbass in its entirety as a condition for any peace deal.
In recent weeks, US President Donald Trump's administration has sought to revive talks to end the four-year-old conflict – Europe's bloodiest since World War Two.
The US leader last month urged Ukraine to refrain from hitting Russian oil installations, saying that was sending global diesel prices surging.
But Zelenskyy, speaking as air raid sirens blared outside the gilded halls of the presidential offices, said he had received no indications from Russia that Putin was interested in peace talks, or discussing a ceasefire on energy infrastructure.
Over the past week, the Ukrainian capital has come under persistent attack by Russian drones and missiles targeting energy and telecoms assets, road and rail infrastructure.
For the first time, Russia has targeted the bridges across the Dnipro river connecting east and west Kiev.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine would react to the change in tactics by Moscow, but would not target civilian infrastructure indiscriminately.
"We have to respond in any way (we can). With their attacks on our energy, we have to respond on their energy. First of all, oil refiners etc: what gives money to them for this war," Zelenskyy said in English.
"But we will not respond, of course, just like them, on any civilian objects."

articles.title: Russia has reduced use of ballistic missiles ahead of winter – Dutch analyst
articles.body:
Russia has reduced use of ballistic missiles ahead of winter – Dutch analyst
He expressed this opinion in an exclusive comment to Ukrinform. Bolder is a strategic analyst and defense expert at the Hague Center for Strategic Studies (HCSS) and a former lieutenant colonel in the Royal Netherlands Air Force.
Bolder said that Russia was currently escalating its attacks on Ukrainian territory and that these attacks were having a severe impact on the lives of ordinary Ukrainian civilians. He said this was horrific. According to the analyst, the main weapons Russia was currently using were the Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet-powered drones. Ukraine did not yet have a complete response to these drones, although it was making very active efforts to destroy them as well. The effectiveness of intercepting them was gradually increasing and had already exceeded 50%.
At the same time, Bolder noted that the number of ballistic missiles Russia was using was currently lower than before. In his view, this suggested that, as Ukraine did not yet have a real response to the jet-powered drones, Russia was refraining from using ballistic missiles and was likely saving them for further use during the winter.
He also drew attention to the development of Ukrainian ballistic missile capabilities. In his view, the creation of such systems could have a dual significance: in addition to providing Ukraine with the ability to strike Russian launchers, it would give the country a technological foundation for developing its own interceptor missiles.
At the same time, he identified the need to scale up production of such systems to sufficient volumes as the key challenge.
The analyst also warned of possible problems for Ukraine in winter. He said these could affect not only electricity supplies, as the country had a significant number of generators, but also the operation of water treatment and sewage systems, as well as electricity supplies to defense industry enterprises.
In his assessment, the intensification of strikes on civilian infrastructure could be linked to the situation on the battlefield, where Russian forces, he said, were suffering significant losses and had recently lost some territory.
Bolder said that a serious problem was that businesses were being left without electricity. He said that, in effect, Russia wanted to suffocate Ukraine and make the Ukrainian economic model unviable for a very long time so that Ukraine would eventually become exhausted. At the same time, he said, efforts were also being made to persuade Europe to stop supporting Ukraine, leaving it with no choice but to accept Putin's demands. However, he noted that history showed this never worked that way: the more strongly one state attacked a people or another country, the more people rallied around their flag.

articles.title: Israel blows up schools, flattens villages in southern Lebanon
articles.body:
Israel blows up schools, flattens villages in southern Lebanon
TEHRAN — Israeli forces escalated their campaign of artillery shelling, airstrikes, and controlled demolitions across southern Lebanon over the weekend, turning border villages into uninhabitable wreckage while Washington provides political cover for the ongoing aggression.
Explosives in schools and destruction of border villages
According to local media outlets, the latest wave of destruction hit hardest in the Marjayoun and Tyre districts. In Houla, Israeli soldiers rigged a private school building with heavy explosives before blowing it up and setting fire to nearby homes.
Similar demolitions shook Al-Mansouri, where massive detonations sent clouds of white smoke rising above residential neighborhoods, rattling windows as far away as Tyre. The town’s public school had already been mostly destroyed during earlier raids.
Lebanese news outlets also reported relentless artillery bombardment across Wadi Al-Hujeir, Nabatieh Al-Fawqa, Kfarromman, and Baraachit. Israeli warplanes launched strikes on Kfar Tebnit, Bani Hayyan, and the outskirts of Mayfadoun and Zawtar al-Sharqiyah, while low-flying fighter jets buzzed towns across the south.
According to local reports, Israeli troops currently occupy more than 60 southern communities, carrying out systematic demolitions to ensure civilian populations cannot return.
The American shield and occupation costs
This campaign continues despite the “Framework Agreement” signed in Washington on June 26. Advertised by American officials as a step toward Israeli withdrawal and Lebanese army deployment, the deal has produced no pullback.
Instead, Tel Aviv has used the agreement to entrench its presence while demanding unilateral Lebanese concessions.
The ongoing occupation poses severe daily hazards for local populations trying to check their land. On September 30, a Lebanese army serviceman was severely injured alongside three civilians near Nabatieh al-Fawqa when a leftover explosive charge detonated during a property inspection escort.
Israeli forces are not operating without cost. An Israeli military spokesperson confirmed Sunday that an officer was moderately injured and a soldier seriously hurt in an operational explosion in southern Lebanon on Friday.
Meanwhile, figures cited from Israel’s war ministry show that 1,318 Israeli military and security personnel have died across all battlefronts since October 2023.

articles.title: German chancellor in Kyiv calls on Putin to "stop this senseless war"
articles.body:
German chancellor in Kyiv calls on Putin to "stop this senseless war"
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who is visiting Kyiv, has called on Russian ruler Vladimir Putin to stop attacks on Ukraine and demonstrate a readiness to negotiate.
Source: German news agency dpa, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Merz, accompanied by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, visited the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine in Kyiv, which had been damaged in a drone strike.
During Merz's visit, air-raid warnings were issued several times due to Russian attacks, while the Pivnichnyi (North) Bridge had been damaged earlier that morning.

Details: Standing near the damaged National Academy of Sciences building, the chancellor said that attacks such as the one that took place last Monday clearly demonstrate the senselessness of the war.
"An attack on the Academy of Sciences in Kyiv, in the middle of the city, just a few hundred metres from the German embassy. And this morning, on a peaceful Sunday, an air-raid alarm in Kyiv. These are daily war crimes being committed here," he noted.
Merz said that while Ukraine is preparing for winter, its infrastructure is being attacked every day.
"I appeal once again to the Russian leadership, to the Russian president: Stop this war! We can talk, but only when the weapons fall silent – and the weapons must fall silent," he said. [N.B. Ukrainska Pravda does not recognise Putin as president – ed.]

articles.title: Valdai 2026: The search for a new world order has only just begun
articles.body:
Valdai 2026: The search for a new world order has only just begun
Journalists and public figures from nearly 40 countries gathered at this year’s Valdai Club conference to discuss how the world is responding to a growing number of crises, and one conclusion stood out – the world has become more complex and there will be no return to an age of simple solutions.
The 20th century gave humanity a great deal, but it also encouraged the belief that fundamental political and social questions can be settled by choosing the correct ideology. Capitalism and communism competed to provide the answer, and after the Cold War, liberal globalism made its own attempt to reduce international affairs to a common set of rules and assumptions, but this has also failed.
We are therefore learning to live in a world where even the most dangerous developments need not produce panic or despair. This was reflected in the agenda at Valdai as participants discussed issues that would have seemed extraordinary 15 or 20 years ago about how societies withstand prolonged war, the increasingly impersonal nature of modern warfare, the military use of AI, and the uncertain future of nuclear deterrence.
Yet these discussions took place without a sense of panic, and without attempts to frighten participants with the prospect of a world in which the US and Europe can no longer set the rules. As Russian President Vladimir Putin argued in the closing session, the global situation under these circumstances could instead change for the better.
This explains why, despite the dangers facing the world, the tone at Valdai was constructive. Yes, the risks are real, but they were discussed as conditions in which future development must take place, rather than as signs of inevitable catastrophe.
One reason is that the overwhelming majority of participants come from countries outside the West, and their perspective is often quite different from that which prevails in Europe, as rather than seeking to restore an international order that is disappearing, they’re trying to understand what will replace it.
In this respect, Valdai provides a useful snapshot of the intellectual debate taking place beyond the Western world.
For Russia, this matters enormously, given new ideas and alternative approaches to development are increasingly being debated in China, India, Iran, and the Arab world, and across Africa, Asia, and Latin America, and Russia has much to learn from these discussions.
It’s equally important to understand the thinking of countries that have resisted pressure from the US and Europe and maintained relations with Russia during the past four years. These countries constitute much of the ‘global majority’ with which Russia hopes to build a multipolar international order.
The exchange also gives Russia the opportunity to explain its own perspective, not only on the Ukraine conflict but on broader questions that will shape international affairs for decades, and the first is war.
International law is playing a diminishing role in restraining countries, as conflicts in some regions have become exceptionally violent, while new technologies are changing the nature of warfare, and unmanned systems and AI create possibilities that scarcely existed a generation ago. Far from eliminating human responsibility, these technologies make questions of responsibility, error, and human judgment even more important.
The second question is how international rules will be established and maintained as Western influence declines.
Russia, China, and other countries have long promoted multipolarity as an alternative model of international order. Putin used his Valdai appearance to call for reform of the UN system and a greater role for developing countries and the Global South in making important international decisions.
The third challenge is older but no less pressing because climate change, environmental degradation, inequality, and poverty have not disappeared, and while the struggle by the US and Europe to preserve their international position has increasingly pushed these questions into the background, they will eventually have to be addressed.
This raises two difficult questions regarding the role China and other Asian powers will play, and which institutions will be capable of coordinating international action.
There is still no clear answer to the first, and Asian countries show little enthusiasm for simply replacing the West as global leaders, but on the second, BRICS increasingly appears capable of playing an important role.
The attraction of BRICS is that it does not operate through one member issuing instructions to the other, and that its members have different interests and political systems but share an interest in stable development and greater freedom in determining their own policies.
Its weaknesses should not be ignored, because BRICS lacks the internal discipline characteristic of traditional Western alliances, and two of its members, Iran and the UAE, came dangerously close to conflict this spring, yet the organization is increasingly discussed as a source of mutually beneficial ideas and practical solutions.
Another challenge is AI, and this goes far beyond its military uses. Fundamental questions concern the ethical limits of AI, the preservation of humanism, and the danger of what Putin calls “digital totalitarianism.” Technological progress is moving faster than the political and social institutions that are expected to regulate it.
For Russia, perhaps the most important lesson is that the economic and social problems it faces aren’t uniquely Russian, given that countries everywhere are struggling with economic imbalance, technological disruption, and rapid social change, and this is both good and bad news.
It’s good news for Russia because it demonstrates the failure of Western attempts since 2022 to isolate the country from the wider world, but it’s bad news because nobody has discovered universal solutions to these problems.
Economic and social resilience will therefore be critical, as the international system is undergoing changes on a scale rarely seen in modern history. An era lasting more than 500 years, during which Western civilization progressively acquired the ability to determine much of humanity’s political and economic development, is coming to an end, and this transformation coincides with extraordinary advances in technology, medicine, and genetics.
Every major civilization is searching for answers, but the fundamental disagreement concerns how these answers should be found, as Western countries are attempting to preserve the international positions they have accumulated over centuries, while Russia and its partners in BRICS argue instead for an order based on sovereign choice and mutual benefit.
The clash between these two approaches may prove to be the defining conflict of our time.
This article was first published by Vzglyad.ru, translated and edited by the RT team.

articles.title: Ukraine to Close Its Current Budget Deficit by Year’s End
articles.body:
Ukraine will eliminate its wartime budget deficit before the end of the year, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced in an interview with Reuters.
Zelensky stated that negotiations conducted by Ukrainian officials in Brussels had produced a viable framework to manage the state’s short-term financing gap while maintaining steady procurement for the armed forces.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Over the past several months we worked on our financial deficit. We will close the current deficit by the end of the year,” Zelensky said in comments released by the presidential administration. “We still have some issues to work through, but we will close the deficit.”
The president described resolving the shortfall as a major success for Ukraine, his negotiating team, and European partners, emphasizing that stabilization of the state budget was achieved through joint fiscal adjustments and credit mechanisms.
Frontloading EU loans and 2027 drone contracts
Zelensky explained that the government intends to advance portions of European credit allocations originally scheduled for 2027 into early January, ensuring that domestic defense contractors receive early capital allocations to maintain uninterrupted production lines.
“It was not easy. We worked with our budget, with our partners, especially the European Union, and we will also try to partially use loan funds for next year,” Zelensky said. “We will bring this closer to January and use this money to order drones for January and February 2027. My team returned from Brussels and reported. Everything is working well. I hope that this will continue.”
Vilnius Airport Closes as NATO Jets Scramble Over Suspected Drone
The drive to secure early procurement funding follows discussions between Ukrainian economic officials and European counterparts in Brussels, where Ukrainian Finance Minister Serhiy Marchenko outlined long-term financing requirements for the coming fiscal year.
Marchenko previously cautioned that Ukraine could face a prospective financial shortfall of approximately €69 billion ($78 billion) in 2027, projecting requirements of roughly €40 billion ($45 billion) for defense operations and €29 billion ($33 billion) to maintain civilian state administration and public services.
Reform conditionality and frozen asset discussions
The planned deployment of credit lines unfolds as Brussels manages disbursements under the EU’s €90 billion ($102 billion) support loan facility covering the 2026-2027 period.
Under the framework’s 2026 allocation of €45 billion ($51 billion), the European Commission has disbursed approximately €15 billion ($17 billion). European officials have emphasized that subsequent payment tranches remain linked to verified reform benchmarks, focusing on anti-corruption enforcement, judicial governance, and public administration transparency.
European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos noted during donor coordination sessions that completing statutory reforms remains the primary mechanism for unlocking committed funding pipelines, urging Ukrainian institutions to coordinate closely to meet technical criteria.
Concurrently, European capitals have debated proposals to utilize immobilized Russian sovereign assets to support Ukraine’s defense and recovery.
While Kyiv has advocated using portions of the roughly €210 billion ($239 billion) in Russian central bank reserves immobilized across Europe – principally held in Belgium through the Euroclear depository – member states including Belgium, France, and Italy have urged caution regarding potential legal liabilities and financial market stability.
To supplement bilateral budgetary aid, European institutions are also integrating Ukraine into wider industrial initiatives. The European Commission approved €325 million ($368.6 million) to fund five European Defence Projects of Common Interest (EDPCI), with Ukraine participating in four collaborative frameworks.

articles.body:

Russia May Be Running Secret Mesh Relays Inside Kyiv to Guide Shahed Strikes
Russian forces may be using a small number of radio relay devices operating inside Kyiv to establish temporary communication links with Shahed-type attack drones and adjust their flight during strikes, according to Ukrainian defense technology adviser Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Beskrestnov said on October 3 that he believes Russian Mesh radio relays are periodically activated in the Ukrainian capital, potentially providing a short-term control channel for incoming drones.
“Right now, I insist that enemy Mesh radio relays are being switched on in Kyiv, providing a temporary short-term control channel for Shaheds to adjust strikes. Not many. Perhaps one to three. Such relays are difficult to find, but they must be searched for,” Beskrestnov said.
According to Beskrestnov, the presence of such devices could complicate efforts to protect Kyiv using electronic warfare systems, as the drones could retain a communication channel during the final stage of an attack.
He pointed to previous Russian strikes in Kyiv, including an attack on a Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) building, as evidence supporting his assessment.
“At the moment of the strike, there were no other Shahed relay drones in the sky. I also analyzed other strikes on Kyiv bridges and the possibility of organizing long-range Mesh channels from Russia at those moments,” he said.
Beskrestnov also raised concerns about Russian access to information on the location of Ukrainian air defense systems deployed around critical infrastructure. Images showing air defense equipment on Kyiv bridges have circulated online, while such deployments are difficult to conceal because tens of thousands of people use the crossings daily, he said.
As long as Russia maintains the ability to control Shahed drones in real time, Beskrestnov said, both infrastructure and air defense systems could potentially be targeted.
He argued that accurately striking individual structural elements of a bridge, such as supports or cables, would require a stable control channel that remains active until the final stage of the drone’s flight.
Beskrestnov stressed that his assessment of Russian relay devices operating inside Kyiv remains a hypothesis. Ukrainian specialists continue examining debris from downed Russian drones for evidence of alternative communication systems.
“Let me be wrong in my opinion about the relays,” Beskrestnov said. “I also want to say that we carefully examine all debris. We do not find any other ‘secret’ means of communication.”
The assessment follows earlier concerns over relay infrastructure outside Ukraine. On September 29, Ukraine’s State Border Guard Service said Belarus periodically activates relay systems that can strengthen communications for Russian drones during attacks on Ukraine.
In June, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called on Belarusian leader Alexander Lukashenko to dismantle relay equipment that Kyiv said was being used to support Russian drone operations.

This morning, I was glad to welcome Chancellor Friedrich Merz to Kyiv. Today, he will hold talks with President @ZelenskyyUa on all matters of our bilateral, European, and international agenda. Thank you for coming to Ukraine at… pic.twitter.com/brwmmtQYsw
— Andrii Sybiha 🇺🇦 (@andrii_sybiha) October 4, 2026
Domestic political headwinds
Merz’s unannounced visit follows repeated warnings from Berlin that air defense shortfalls represent the primary threat to Ukraine’s wartime resilience ahead of the heating season.
Speaking in Berlin on Sept. 29, Merz described territorial air defense as Ukraine’s “weakest point,” confirming that the German government has engaged in intensive diplomatic consultations with European partners to assemble emergency military packages ahead of the European Council summit in Brussels on Oct. 15-16.
The chancellor has framed continued military assistance to Kyiv as an imperative for continental stability. During a recent address in Münster, Merz argued that Western strength and unity remain prerequisites for any future peace negotiations with the Kremlin, cautioning that a Russian-dictated peace would destabilize the continent, trigger mass refugee movements, and leave Europe structurally insecure.
The high-profile trip also unfolds against acute domestic political friction within Germany, where populist and pro-Kremlin factions have mobilized voter discontent over economic pressures and military spending.
The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) – which opposes arms shipments to Kyiv and demands an immediate resumption of Russian natural gas imports – achieved historic electoral gains in September, capturing roughly 44 percent of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt before securing first place in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
Despite rising electoral polarization, Merz reaffirmed that Germany will not waver in its defense commitments to Ukraine, arguing that protecting Kyiv’s sovereignty remains the baseline foundation for Germany’s own long-term peace and economic prosperity.

articles.title: Iran says Hormuz will not reopen until conditions are met
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran says Strait of Hormuz will not reopen until conditions are met
The Strait of Hormuz will not reopen until seven Iranian conditions set out in a June interim agreement with the US are met, state media reported Iran's parliament speaker Mohammad Baqer Ghalibaf as saying on Sunday.
Iran presented a proposal during the UN General Assembly under which the Strait of Hormuz waterway could be reopened and normal maritime passage restored within seven days if the conditions were met, with the US replying to this proposal last week via Qatari intermediaries.
"The position of the Islamic Republic of Iran is completely clear and firm, and the Strait of Hormuz will not be opened until our seven conditions, based on the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, are met," Ghalibaf, who is Iran's top negotiator, was quoted as saying.
He said Washington "must understand that the period of dragging out the (diplomatic) process and dictating one-sided demands is over".
Iran says no nuclear discussions
A Foreign Ministry spokesperson said on Sunday that Tehran had clarified its broad positions via mediators to the US response but that additional points remained to be communicated to Washington.
"The Americans' propositions are more or less in line with their previous positions, specifically on the nuclear issue. We told them our focus in this stage is the issue of the Strait of Hormuz and the return to security in this waterway requires clear steps from the US," spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said.
He also denied Tehran had offered UN nuclear watchdog inspections of its nuclear facilities in exchange for US sanctions relief, saying Iran had not entered into nuclear discussions with Washington.
The document being circulated outlines a seven-day period of trust-building aimed at returning the two sides to an enhanced version of the memorandum of understanding agreed in June, including concrete steps on Iran's nuclear programme, an official briefed on the talks said last week.
The disagreement centres on the sequencing of the steps rather than the components of the plan, the official added.
Warning from Araghchi
Qatar has been shuttling messages between Washington and Tehran in an effort to end the conflict and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, the conduit for a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas before the war that began at the end of February with US and Israeli attacks on Iran.
The June memorandum of understanding led to a brief ceasefire and included provisions on the strait and Iran's nuclear programme.
Separately, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told foreign ambassadors and diplomats in Tehran on Sunday that Tehran hoped Washington would choose diplomacy but warned that Iran was prepared to respond if the US again chose military action.
On Thursday, sources told Reuters that Iran was preparing a broader and more forceful response if Washington resumed large-scale military attacks.
“If they again move towards military solutions, we are more prepared than before and will take whatever action is necessary to defend ourselves,” Araghchi said on Sunday.
Army spokesperson Mohammad Akraminia told Fars news agency on Sunday Iran would upgrade the range of its missiles.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: Germany provides Ukraine with $1.46B support package
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Sunday that Germany had provided Ukraine with a new support package worth more than €1.3 billion ($1.46 billion) during talks with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
In a statement on US social media company X, Zelenskyy said the package includes weapons and support for Ukraine’s energy sector ahead of winter.
“It includes weapons that will help us now, as well as support for our energy sector ahead of winter – an important energy package. Of course, we discussed the need for air defence, which is critical at this time,” he said.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine and Germany had signed 15 agreements and documents, most covering security cooperation, defence production, procurement, orders for German industry and joint projects in Ukraine.
“The total value of our agreements today is more than €8.5 billion,” he said, adding that a separate agreement would expand cooperation on joint efforts to counter drones.
Merz arrived in the Ukrainian capital on Sunday morning for an unannounced visit, saying he had traveled to Kiev with the message: “You can rely on us.”
Separately, Zelenskyy said that the United States wants to broker a new round of talks with Ukraine and Russia on ending the four-and-a-half-year war and hold it by the end of October.
"The American side is currently in contact with Ukraine and Russia and is proposing to somehow hold a meeting at the technical level in a trilateral format by the end of October," Zelenskyy told reporters.

articles.title: Reaching the core: could Russia cut Ukrainians off from the internet and mobile communications?
articles.body:
Reaching the core: could Russia cut Ukrainians off from the internet and mobile communications?
Over the past week, the Kremlin has been expanding its campaign of terror to include new targets. In addition to hitting energy infrastructure and logistics hubs, Russia is now attacking the data centres that house equipment used by internet service providers, government services, banks and other digital systems, launching a wave of strikes on buildings where vital telecoms infrastructure is concentrated.
Telecoms industry representatives say it is not possible to cut Kyiv or Ukraine off from the internet by hitting data centres. There is no single facility whose destruction would take the country offline. But the objective of these attacks is not merely to carry out acts of terror. The goal is not the total destruction of the internet, but to degrade internet quality and overload backup routes, which could increase latency and destabilise networks.
And that may not be the worst-case scenario. The Russians have also started targeting mobile operator infrastructure, which may have more far-reaching consequences. Could these attacks disrupt communications across Ukraine? Where are the weak points in the country's telecoms infrastructure, and why is it that mobile networks could turn out to be significantly more vulnerable? Read on to find out.
From data centres to mobile network operators
On 23 September, Russian drones attacked a building in central Kyiv that housed one of the capital's data centres. A business centre was hit by several jet-powered Shahed drones in the course of an hour, and a fire then broke out.
Later that day, drones struck a similar data centre in another part of the city, and that evening, Russian forces hit yet another facility housing a data centre.
In one day, Russia had attacked at least three data centres in different parts of Kyiv. All housed equipment belonging to internet service providers. Some, notably the cloud service Fex.net, reported disruptions to their services. Ukraine's Ministry of Digital Transformation said around 100,000 users had problems accessing the internet.
Ekonomichna Pravda estimates that at least nine data centres in Kyiv may have been targeted since September, some of them more than once. The Protasiv Yar business centre, which housed the Cosmonova data centre, has been hit twice. Cosmonova suspended operations at the site as a result.
Four days later, the Russians turned their attention to mobile operators' infrastructure. Kyivstar, Ukraine's largest mobile operator, reported that a drone had struck one of its buildings, and Russia's Defence Ministry claimed that equipment belonging to Vodafone Ukraine had been damaged.
Internet service providers and mobile operators have suffered attacks to their networks before, but since 23 September the attacks have been on a different scale. Several data centres were hit within a few days, including some facilities that are critical to the telecoms industry.
For instance, a Russian attack destroyed a data centre that housed infrastructure belonging to hosting provider MiroHost. Founder Oleksandr Olshanskyi said MiroHost won't be able to bring its Ukraine-based infrastructure back online for at least the next three months.
Government digital services have also been disrupted, including state registries and electronic registration at centres run by Ukraine's Ministry of Internal Affairs that provide administrative services related to vehicles and driving licences.
The attacks on data centres have affected television broadcasts too. Disruptions have been reported by Army TV, Novyny.Live, We Are Ukraine, Pershyi, STB, 1+1, Channel 5, Suspilne Sport and Suspilne Culture.
Further evidence of the attacks is contained in a video posted by the Varyag Brigade, which is regarded as one of Russia's elite drone units alongside the better-known Rubicon unit. In the footage, Russian military personnel claim to have struck at least 11 data centres in Kyiv.
The exact dates of the strikes shown in the video cannot be established, but some appear to have taken place between 23 and 27 September. The footage clearly shows a strike on the Datagroup data centre on 25 September.
Read more: Fahrenheit 451: Russia has destroyed one-third of the books printed in Ukraine this year
The Ukrainian authorities had to respond. Following a meeting of the Staff of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said specific decisions had been taken to protect data centres and other critical communications infrastructure. The government is preparing for the worst. Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said the risk of widespread internet disruptions will persist for as long as Russia continues its strikes.
There is no one-size-fits-all way to protect this infrastructure. Some equipment can be moved underground; some can migrate to cloud environments or be relocated abroad. For some systems, a combination of these approaches may be used.
The government has allocated UAH 518.3 million (about US$11.5 million) to establish backup environments at separate locations, cloud infrastructure, and additional sites for state information systems. The funds will also be used to purchase server equipment, software, and data backup and recovery systems.
What happens if a data centre is attacked?
Much of the digital infrastructure Ukrainians rely on every day is built around data centres. The servers and storage systems they house keep websites, apps, state registers and banking services running.
Data centres are critical for internet service providers, as they house essential resources such as web, email and Domain Name System (DNS) servers, cloud infrastructure, and equipment belonging to providers and their clients.
Dmytro Kokhmaniuk, an expert on internet infrastructure and DNS, says some companies rent capacity in several data centres, others have their own facilities, and some combine both approaches. Spreading infrastructure across multiple sites helps make networks more resilient.
Repairing a data centre after an attack is a complex and lengthy process. "It's not just a room full of servers," Kokhmaniuk says. "It's a vast engineering system that includes a power supply, generators, cooling systems, ventilation, physical access control and network infrastructure. Damage to one or more of these elements can render the entire facility inoperable."
Consequently, a strike on a data centre can disrupt its operations even if the servers themselves escape damage. That does not necessarily mean, however, that the data stored there would be lost.
If up-to-date backups are stored at another independent site, the data can be restored. But getting everything back up and running requires computing resources, system configuration, and time. The impact of an attack therefore depends on how the particular service is set up and operated.
Since the start of Russia's full-scale war, a significant proportion of Ukraine's state registers and digital infrastructure has been moved to cloud services and backup environments in other countries.
So even if Russia destroys a Ukrainian data centre, the resulting outage may not last long. The attack may, however, cause temporary disruptions, loss of access and damage to equipment, and make it necessary to repair or relocate infrastructure.
Internet connectivity must also be restored separately. Damage to routers or an internet provider's cables can cut users off even when the service itself continues to operate. In that case, access can be restored using backup routes and equipment that survived intact, or by repairing the damaged network.
Internet speeds may drop
The events of 23 September offer some insight into what Russia may be trying to achieve by targeting Ukrainian network infrastructure.
One of the organisations affected that day was the internet service provider Pavutyna, which notified users of disruptions to its network. Co-owner and director Oleksandr Arutiunian said it was the third strike on the company's infrastructure, but the latest attack hit equipment at several locations almost simultaneously.
"The first two attacks were less disruptive because the backup systems worked better and the damage didn't all happen at the same time," Arutiunian says. "During the third attack, two locations were hit at once. The network could not recover automatically, so some users were left without a connection for between one and two hours. Repair crews then brought the network back online."
It appears that the Russians' target is not so much individual government services as the infrastructure that provides internet access. To this end, they are striking large data centres that house equipment used by several providers.
The telecoms industry representatives interviewed by Ekonomichna Pravda say these attacks cannot cut Ukrainians off from the internet entirely, because providers' network nodes are not only located in data centres.
"Networks have become much more decentralised in recent years," Arutiunian explains. "An operator can have far more than just one, two or five nodes. If necessary, backup equipment can be deployed at another site. In many cases this happens automatically, and engineers only need to step in when the damage is more serious."
If Ukrainian networks have numerous connections and backup routes, then what can Russia realistically achieve by attacking data centres?
Ekonomichna Pravda's sources say providers' network nodes and internet exchange points (IXPs) could potentially be targets. Network nodes support the operation of providers' networks, while IXPs allow different networks to exchange data. There are around 20 IXPs in Ukraine, and their equipment can be located at a single site or several.
The destruction of some of these facilities would not result in a nationwide internet blackout. As long as alternative connections are intact, internet service providers could reroute traffic through other operators, direct connections and international IXPs, just as traffic is diverted when a road is closed. Networks without an alternative route, however, could lose connectivity if their infrastructure is damaged.
The problem may lie elsewhere. Backup routes often have less capacity and are not set up to handle additional traffic. This could result in slower internet speeds and dropped connections for users.
That is what happened to internet provider Fiberlink after Russian attacks damaged the infrastructure of one of its backbone partners. The company rerouted traffic through a backup channel and warned users that internet speeds could temporarily drop. Further damage could lead to more significant disruptions.
According to Kokhmaniuk, poorer connection quality and slower data transfer speeds could be likely. In any event, operators will also have to absorb the additional cost of repairing infrastructure, deploying emergency repair crews and constructing backup lines. If the attacks continue, this could ultimately drive up the cost of broadband for subscribers.
"Operators will need to decentralise their networks further and expand the number of nodes and backup sites, which will increase the cost of providing services," Arutiunian says. "They will need more equipment, more staff and more resources to maintain and support this infrastructure."
Mobile network operator infrastructure
Mobile communications are another area of concern. If Russia continues to hit facilities belonging to mobile network operators, as it did on 27 September, this could have more serious consequences than attacks on data centres.
The Russians would not need to strike tens of thousands of base stations. The mobile core network, which manages subscriber registration, calls, text messages and mobile internet access, may be a far more vulnerable target.
If attacks were to disrupt critical functions of a core network beyond what its backup systems can handle, the consequences could be similar to those of the cyberattack on Kyivstar, which left millions of subscribers without access to calls, text messages or mobile internet.
Operators maintain backup infrastructure, but a fully-fledged mobile core network cannot simply be replicated by installing spare equipment at another node. Ekonomichna Pravda's sources estimate that building an additional core could cost each operator US$40-50 million. How many layers of redundancy would be needed if attacks on this infrastructure became sustained is an open question.
Ekonomichna Pravda's sources say the state and operators are taking steps to build more redundancy into critical network components. Some of these measures have been introduced only recently and will take time to implement. Russian attacks on mobile infrastructure could therefore pose a greater risk to communications.
What does this mean for users? In a critical situation, it's best to have more than one way of accessing the internet – for example, broadband from one provider and mobile internet from another. The more independent connections there are, the lower the risk of losing access during a large-scale attack.
Translated by Artem Yakymyshyn
Edited by Teresa Pearce

All EU member state embassies remain in Kyiv, EU ambassador to Ukraine says
EU Ambassador to Ukraine Katarína Mathernová has said that all European Union member state embassies will continue operating in Kyiv despite Russian threats.

Mathernová noted that Russia is trying to make the EU reduce its support for Ukraine, but that this only makes the EU more determined to continue that support. She pointed out that the Vienna Conventions govern the operation of diplomatic missions worldwide, and said Russia would be better off not testing their strength.
Background:
- The EU recently condemned Russia's nuclear threats against NATO member states.

articles.title: A Nobel laureate’s deal: free Russia’s prisoners, fund the missiles hitting Ukraine
articles.body:
Dmitry Muratov, the Nobel Peace Prize laureate and co-founder of Russia's shuttered Novaya Gazeta, has lent his name to an idea that sounds like pure humanitarianism. Russia frees some of the people it jails for opposing the war; in return, the United States eases its sanctions on the Russian economy.
The scheme did not even start in an American office. According to The Atlantic, which reported the plan on 29 September, it was Muratov himself who urged Donald Trump's envoy, John Coale, to try it. Coale had used the same model on Belarus, where some 500 prisoners were released, sanctions softened, and trade talks reopened.
Now, with Trump's approval, he wants to run it on the Kremlin.
“A direct investment in ammunition flying across the border”: Belarusian defectors warn US sanctions relief is funding Russia’s war
The prisoners should go free. There is nothing to argue about there. No one jailed for anti-war words, for journalism, or for political dissent belongs in a cell. But here is the small detail: the price for their freedom is easing the pressure on a state that is waging war, not on the United States, which is being asked to ease the sanctions, but on Ukraine.
And here is where the real humanitarian arithmetic begins. We do not yet know which sanctions would be lifted. Whichever they are, the logic is the same: Moscow lets some of its political prisoners go, and Washington gives the Russian economy some breathing room in return. People walk out of Russian prisons, and the Kremlin gets more oxygen.
More money for the Russian state in wartime is not merely a figure in a bank report. It is more resources for the army, for missiles, for drones, for the war's continuation. And Ukrainians are the ones who feel it.
I can picture the Kremlin ghoul rubbing his hands at an idea like this. Now he can be not just president, but the director of a prisoner market: release a hundred today, jail three hundred tomorrow, so there is something to trade next time. New dissidents, journalists, activists, and merely inconvenient citizens he can pack away far faster than the West can lift a sanction.
A tidy little business model: Russia produces the prisoners, the West buys them back with its policy, and Ukraine settles the account.
Because if easing sanctions widens Russia's room to finance the war, then Ukrainians effectively get a very strange bill for someone else's humanism: a Russian political prisoner walks out of prison, and a Ukrainian gets a fresh portion of missiles and drones on their head.
By the way, about those Ukrainian civilians. By the estimates of international and Ukrainian rights groups, Russia is holding, or has held, some 16,000 of them illegally. The real figure may be higher, since not every case can be documented.
This is exactly where Muratov, as a Nobel peace laureate, might find his powers of persuasion useful. Why not put in a word for the Ukrainians in Russian prisons? The same people seized in occupied territory during "filtration," taken from their homes, buried under fabricated cases, held for years without a proper trial.
And among them are children.
And here onto the stage steps Russia's Baba Yaga of "child protection": Maria Lvova-Belova, the so-called presidential commissioner for children's rights. She herself told Putin, in public, about a boy from Mariupol she had taken into her care after he was removed from the occupied city. Ukraine and international organizations view such cases as part of a wider system of unlawful transfers of Ukrainian children to Russia. The International Criminal Court has issued a warrant for her arrest on exactly those charges: the unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children.
That is what Russian care for children looks like: take a Ukrainian child from Mariupol, carry him off to Russia, and set about turning him into a Russian. If this is how Russia's children's commissioner works in public, it is frightening to imagine what happens where there are no cameras and no international warrants.
Nobody is offering to lift a single sanction for them.
And Muratov's pacifist initiatives are not new, either. After the full-scale invasion, he was among the authors and promoters of the ceasefire appeals. One public statement, signed by 51 Nobel laureates, called for an end to the fighting, which Muratov later described as a plea for a "genuine ceasefire" before talks.
On paper it all looks wonderful: stop shooting, stop killing one another, make peace. But there is one small problem. Russia did not wander into this war alongside Ukraine. Russia launched the full-scale invasion itself.
And in these appeals, Muratov did not demand that the Kremlin withdraw its troops from Ukraine. He did not demand the de-occupation of Ukrainian territory. He did not put the question of responsibility for the aggression and the war crimes to Russia. The formula was far more convenient: just stop shooting.
But "stop killing each other" is a beautiful phrase for people who would rather not notice who attacked whom.
It turns aggressor and victim into two symmetrical sides, as though Ukraine and Russia had simply quarreled and now both must show wisdom and stop firing. There is just one nuance: if, after such a "peace," the Russian army remains on occupied Ukrainian territory, that is not an end to the aggression. It is a pause with a Russian flag on Ukrainian soil.
Now add the prisoner proposal on top. Russia does not withdraw its troops. Ukraine does not get its occupied territory back. The Kremlin answers for nothing. But a few Russian political prisoners are released, and for that, Russia's sanctions are eased too. And Ukraine, meanwhile, is simply supposed to stand to one side and rejoice that humanism has triumphed.
Except there is a difference of principle. A Russian political prisoner can walk out of a Russian prison. A Ukrainian civilian can stay in one. And a Ukrainian soldier can be killed by a weapon Russia bought thanks to that same sanctions relief.
And then a very simple question arises for the great humanist and Nobel laureate: why should the freedom of Russia's political prisoners be bought at the expense of the freedom, the safety, and the lives of Ukrainians?

articles.title: Tory conference 2026: What POLITICO reporters are watching for
articles.body:
BIRMINGHAM, England — Britain’s largest opposition party wants to show it’s still on the electoral pitch during an annual gathering that kicks off Sunday.
Despite Conservative Leader Kemi Badenoch consolidating her position and seeing improved personal ratings, the party is still far from its government heyday, and faces an ongoing challenge on the right from Nigel Farage’s populist Reform UK.
Here’s what POLITICO’s team of reporters will be watching for as the Conservatives gather in Birmingham.
Advertisement
U.K. Political Editor Dan Bloom
My biggest question for Badenoch’s speech at 11 a.m. Wednesday will be: can she end Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s honeymoon?
Since July, Labour has jumped to 26% in the polls while the Tories lag behind Reform on 19%. There will simply be fewer lobbyists and hangers-on than at Labour’s jamboree.
Badenoch will spend this week arguing that Burnham, with his crusade against “40 years of neoliberalism,” has ushered in the kind of classic left-right ideological fight that she relishes. Expect her to bang on about cutting welfare to fund defense — two weak points for Labour. And the self-described “badass Kemi” plans to be more abrasive than Burnham, who went out of his way not to attack anyone in his speech.
I reckon two things will decide if she can cut through: her personal brand, and how far she can differentiate the Tories from Labour and Reform (plus, well, her own party from 2024). She will try to paint the Tories as the party of fiscal responsibility but that’s a crowded marketplace. It’s worked for the Conservatives in the past but we aren’t in two-party politics anymore — though admittedly, the five-party split has become less dramatic since the summer.
There will be economic policy announcements but perhaps not on the scale of last year’s pledge to scrap stamp duty. Badenoch has talked about getting rid of inheritance tax but aides appear to be suggesting an announcement isn’t ready.
I can’t wait to see the peacocking by would-be candidates for a general election. Tory aides are shouting from the hills that they are on a “war footing” and candidate selection is ramping up. Some of the high-profile Tories who were rejected for being too centrist are swerving this year’s conference, but former West Midlands Mayor Andy Street will be prominent on the fringe. Critics complain that Badenoch has bulldozed the transepts off her party’s ideological church.
Advertisement
And, of course, I’d ask questions about a coalition. There is no love lost between the Tories and Reform but all recent polls suggest they would have to team up to have any chance of running a government. Will she pull any punches against Farage … or Restore Britain chief Rupert Lowe, whose vote-splitting might help her in the end?
Senior Foreign and Defense Correspondent Esther Webber
I’ll be really interested to see how the party is positioning itself against what we know so far about Ed Miliband’s agenda as foreign secretary — so whether there’s any dissent over new sanctions introduced by Labour on Israeli E1 settlements.
Miliband has just begun to signal a potentially more conciliatory approach to China as an alternative locus of power and investment versus the U.S., so I’ll be looking at whether the Conservatives think this is a weak point where they can redouble attacks on Labour.
There’s also the question of artificial intelligence regulation and which camp the Tories are situating themselves in. Will they agree with the government on the need for a globally coordinated effort, or back U.S. President Donald Trump’s zero-regulation stance?
Finally, here’s a side plot: Are there any signs that former Home Secretary Priti Patel, traditionally a conference fan favorite, is actually doing anything in her new role in coordinating cooperation between the Tories and other parties internationally?
London Influence Reporter John Johnston
With little detail so far about Burnham’s plans for business, and many corporate execs pondering if Farage’s Reform has hit its peak, this Tory conference will be a vital opportunity for the party to try and show it is building back towards being a credible alternative.
Advertisement
Since the 2024 general election, many businesses and lobbying firms have sent only a skeleton staff to Tory conference. But I’ve heard that extra corporate passes and tickets to the standalone Business Day have been snapped up in the last few months. So, attendance may be healthier — even if most still won’t be splashing out on panel events or exhibition stands.
Business leaders remain skeptical about the prospect of an early general election. But as the official opposition, the Conservatives have the potential to help industry shine a spotlight on concerns and push issues up the political agenda if one comes. At last year’s conference, many public affairs pros felt the Tories lacked the ideas, unity and leadership to do that. My focus this year will be figuring out if that assessment has shifted.
Energy Reporter Abby Wallace
The Conservatives have come a long way from the party that, in government, enshrined net-zero targets in law. Badenoch has been clear about the direction she wants to take the party in: ditching legally-binding climate targets and drilling for more oil and gas in the North Sea.
The party’s leader has even suggested that former colleagues who still support the target will not be welcome back on the Tory benches. I’ll be looking out for whether that U-turn at the top has fully filtered through the party.
While energy bills have surged on the back of war in Iran, the party has been pressing Labour ministers to prioritize cutting costs in the system. For the Conservatives, that means ditching some support for renewables and a bigger role for gas and nuclear in the future. I’ll be keeping an ear on whether there is any pressure from the opposition for ministers to intervene ahead of what will be a difficult winter of price rises too.
The future of the North Sea, including looming decisions on Rosebank and Jackdaw, will no doubt spring up on the fringes — especially after the Conservatives clinched the Aberdeen South by-election following a campaign focused on oil and gas drilling.
Advertisement
Financial Services Reporter Eleanor Myers
Andrew Griffith will be stepping up this party conference, having been promoted to shadow chancellor earlier this year to replace his more mild-mannered colleague Mel Stride.
Griffith was a bigwig in business before he entered parliament, and as a former City minister, I’ll be watching whether he focuses his ire on the prospect of Labour raising bank taxes in the budget, which is now less than a month away.
Griffith will make his big speech on how to get Britain growing again at 2 p.m. Monday. Growth was the favored buzzword of former Chancellor Rachel Reeves, and has been heartily adopted by her successor John Healey, although how to achieve it remains a challenge amid soaring debt and rising interest rates. I’m interested to see whether the Conservatives propose a solution.
Senior Technology Reporter Frank Hersey
This conference is a chance for Badenoch’s team to establish any sort of differentiation between Tory tech policy and that of the other parties. This has been getting harder as parties’ approaches have coalesced. Labour committed to a pro-growth agenda for AI under former Prime Minister Keir Starmer with planned regulatory reforms to match. Tory plans for a social media ban for under-16s were eventually (and reluctantly) grasped by Labour. The Tories were further hemmed in by Reform banking the low-tax, low-regulation space.
I’ll be looking to see if the party can get ahead in any policy areas or if it has to pick new ones to do so. Among all the parties, there’s perhaps most interest in what the Conservatives say on tech — as their policy ideas in this space are feeling overdue.
Senior Trade Reporter Sophie Inge
The fightback against Burnham’s pledge to explore closer ties with the EU is expected to continue in Birmingham, after Badenoch warned that Britain shouldn’t be “having arguments which started 10 years ago.”
Deputy Leader Alex Burghart has already pledged to “reverse” the Brexit reset, warning that plans for an agrifood deal with the bloc risk undermining the U.K.’s trading relationship with the U.S., among other countries.

articles.title: German Chancellor Merz arrives in Kyiv amid Russian attacks
articles.body:
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in Kyiv on Sunday as air raid sirens and explosions sounded across the Ukrainian capital, where another Russian drone strike hit the Northern Bridge over the Dnipro River.
Merz travelled to Ukraine for talks with President Volodymyr Zelensky as Germany prepared further military and energy support and deeper cooperation with Ukraine's defence industry.
Four air raid alerts sounded in Kyiv on Sunday morning, Reuters reported. Air defence systems were also heard operating across the city.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said a strike damaged the roadway of the Northern Bridge and a heating main, disrupting hot water supplies in the Desnyanskyi district. No casualties from the bridge strike had been reported.
The attack marked the second consecutive day that the Northern Bridge had been hit. The Southern Bridge was targeted several times earlier in the week. Major bridges in Kyiv have faced Russian strikes for four consecutive days.
Merz and Zelensky paid tribute to Ukrainian soldiers at a memorial in Independence Square and visited a National Academy of Sciences building damaged in an earlier Russian strike.
"Ukraine is facing decisive weeks. That is why I travelled to Kyiv today with the message: You can rely on us," Merz wrote on X.
German government officials told Reuters that Merz would announce the release of €1 billion in military assistance and €350 million for repairs to Ukraine's energy infrastructure.
Germany and Ukraine are also expected to finalise an agreement on joint drone production. Reuters reported that cooperation is expected to include interceptor drones designed to counter high-speed Russian attack drones. Plans also cover the development and production of weapons with ranges exceeding 1,000km.
Merz travelled with Economy Minister Katherina Reiche and representatives from German companies including Siemens Energy, Hensoldt, Diehl Defence and Quantum Systems.
The chancellor is also expected to raise reforms sought by Ukraine's European partners, including measures against corruption.
Russia's Foreign Ministry said on Saturday that Moscow would continue what it described as retaliatory strikes following Ukrainian attacks inside Russia. It also urged foreign nationals and diplomatic personnel to avoid travelling to Ukraine.
Zelensky said Russia launched 135 attack drones across Ukraine overnight, including more than 50 jet-powered models. He said one person was killed in an attack on a pharmaceutical warehouse in Sumy and six people were injured after a communications facility was struck in Dnipro.
"If Russia is not stopped, sooner or later its war machine will turn against us," Merz said.

articles.title: U.S. Air Force adds $12M for AI agents on doomsday plane
articles.body:
- The U.S. Air Force added $12.1 million to Scale AI's contract for agentic AI on the E-4C Survivable Airborne Operations Center, raising it to $44.3 million.
- The work runs through Nov. 5, 2027, with $5 million in fiscal 2026 research funds obligated at award.
The U.S. Air Force has added $12.1 million to a contract with Scale AI to develop artificial intelligence agents for the E-4C Survivable Airborne Operations Center, the new “doomsday plane” meant to keep U.S. leaders in command of the military, including nuclear forces, if ground command centers are destroyed.
The modification raises the total value of the San Francisco company’s contract from $32.2 million to $44.3 million, the U.S. Department of War said. The work will be done in San Francisco and is expected to run through Nov. 5, 2027. The U.S. Air Force obligated $5 million in fiscal 2026 research and development funds at award.
The notice does not say what tasks the AI agents will perform aboard the aircraft, whether they will run on the plane itself or on ground systems that support it, or how much human control will be built in.
Agentic AI goes a step beyond chatbots that answer questions. These systems can plan and carry out multi-step tasks on their own, such as gathering and sorting information, drafting options or managing workflows, with people supervising or approving key decisions. On a command aircraft packed with communications gear and a battle staff, that could mean helping crews handle large volumes of messages and data during a crisis, though the U.S. Air Force has not described its plans.
The original contract was awarded earlier this year through the Air Force Research Laboratory’s Information Directorate in Rome, New York. The latest modification was issued by the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center at Hanscom Air Force Base, Massachusetts.
The E-4C will replace the E-4B Nightwatch, a fleet of four heavily modified Boeing 747-200s that first flew in the 1970s and serve as the National Airborne Operations Center. The aircraft are hardened against the effects of nuclear blasts and can be refueled in flight, allowing them to stay aloft for long periods while the president, defense secretary and senior commanders direct forces from the air.
Sierra Nevada Corp. won a $13 billion contract in April 2024 to build the replacement. The company bought used Boeing 747-8I airliners from Korean Air and is converting them in Dayton, Ohio, adding protection against radiation and electromagnetic pulse, new communications antennas, computers and mission systems. The first E-4C test aircraft flew on Aug. 7, 2025, and flight and ground testing is continuing through 2026 before mission equipment is installed. Deliveries are scheduled to finish by July 2036.
Scale AI, best known for labeling data used to train AI models, has become a major supplier of AI tools to the U.S. military. In March 2025, it won the Defense Innovation Unit’s Thunderforge project to bring AI agents into military planning and operations, working with Anduril and Microsoft. Earlier this year, the Pentagon’s Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office raised the ceiling on another Scale AI agreement from $100 million to $500 million. Meta holds a minority stake in the company.
