articles.title: Iran vows stronger response to military attack
articles.body:
Iran vows stronger response to military attack
Araghchi says Iran remains ready for a diplomatic solution to US conflict
TEHRAN — Iran is ready for a diplomatic solution to its conflict with the US, but if Washington again chooses a military course, Tehran is more prepared than before to defend itself and will deliver a stronger response, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday.
Addressing ambassadors and representatives of foreign countries based in Tehran at the Foreign Ministry, Araghchi said Iran remained firm and serious on both fronts — defending itself and pursuing diplomacy.
“If our enemies again choose the path of military confrontation, they will receive a stronger response than before, and we will defend ourselves more powerfully than before,” he said. “And if they are seeking diplomatic avenues, we remain ready to reach a just and dignified solution to end this war through diplomacy.”
Araghchi said Iran hoped the US would choose “the path of wisdom and rationality,” stressing that there was no military or sanctions-based solution to the conflict.
“The only solution that can work is a negotiated solution based on justice and fairness, and a dignified and diplomatic solution,” he said, adding that such an approach could provide a final way out of what he described as the “illegal and unjust aggression” launched against Iran.
Diplomatic outreach remains strong
Araghchi also highlighted Iran’s diplomatic activity during the recent UN General Assembly meetings in New York, saying the Iranian delegation had played a strong and effective role.
“I met with 42 foreign ministers, and the president met with 10 heads of state in New York,” he said.
He said Iran had clearly explained its positions in New York and that the level of interest shown by different countries in meeting with Iranian officials, learning about Tehran’s views and hearing its proposals had been “very significant.”
Araghchi said this had demonstrated the failure of what he described as an attempt by some in the US to isolate Iran.
“The perception that some people in the US may have had that they could turn Iran into an isolated country had completely failed,” he said, adding that Iran had acted in New York as “a powerful country respected by the international community” and demonstrated that it continued to have “rational positions” and solutions for both war and peace.
Iranian diplomats, he said, had been highly active at the General Assembly and had conveyed the voice of the Iranian people to the international community.
“We were present in all fields and conveyed the voice of the Iranian people to the world,” Araghchi said, adding that Iran had delivered its people's message in favor of peace and rational solutions.
He also said Tehran had clearly explained its conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, stressing that all of those conditions were consistent with commitments that the US must accept.
Tehran dismisses US claim over Iranian delegation
Araghchi also rejected a claim from the US that the Iranian delegation had been expelled from the country.
“Regardless of whether this claim is true or not, since we went and returned according to our own pre-planned schedule, the claim made by the Americans is truly strange,” he said.
He argued that the claim was contradictory because, on the one hand, it amounted to an admission that the US had violated its obligations as the host country of the United Nations, while on the other hand it demonstrated how angry Washington had become over the presence of the
Iranian delegation in the US.
‘No solution through more sanctions’
Araghchi said the US had already failed both militarily and diplomatically and would gain nothing from imposing additional sanctions.
“The US has lost both in war and in diplomacy in the past,” he said. “Trying new sanctions will also be of no benefit to them. There is no military solution and no solution based on more sanctions.”
He reiterated that Tehran remained prepared for both military defense and diplomacy.
“We remain firm and serious in both areas of defending ourselves and advancing diplomacy,” he said.
Calls on Europe to reconsider its position
Araghchi said he had also held extensive discussions with European countries and described those talks as “very frank.”
“We hope that European countries will reconsider their approach toward the Islamic Republic of Iran,” he said.
He referred to what he described as a significant admission by the NATO secretary-general regarding European involvement in the US war against Iran.
“The admission by the NATO secretary-general that European countries participated in the US war against Iran was a serious admission,” Araghchi said.
According to Araghchi, the NATO chief had explicitly said that more than 5,000 US fighter jets had taken off from bases in Europe to attack Iran.
“We are still waiting for European countries to answer this question: Why did they play an effective role in this war against Iran?” he said.
Despite his criticism, Araghchi said Iran's proposal to European countries was to establish dialogue with Tehran and avoid any participation in renewed efforts by the US and Israel to escalate the conflict.
“Our proposal to these countries is to establish dialogue with the Islamic Republic of Iran and avoid any participation in renewed warmongering by the US and the Zionist regime,” he said.
Seven-day plan could reopen Hormuz
Araghchi said Iran's most important diplomatic initiative was a proposal it had presented for resolving the disputes between Iran and the US and ending the ongoing war.
He referred to the initiative as the seven-day plan, saying that acceptance of the proposal would allow the Strait of Hormuz to be reopened within seven days.
“The most important of all these issues is the plan that the Islamic Republic of Iran has presented for resolving the existing disputes and the ongoing war between Iran and the US,” he said.
“This plan is known as the seven-day plan, and if it is accepted, the Strait of Hormuz will be reopened within seven days.”
Araghchi's remarks came as Tehran reiterated that it remained open to diplomacy while warning that any renewed military action would be met with a stronger response.

articles.title: Moscow vows to ramp up strikes on Ukraine after Zelensky’s threat

In response to a question about Trump’s claim that lack of progress in negotiations with Iran stems from his fundamental uncertainty about who his counterpart within Iran actually is or with whom he should speak, Baghaei pointed out, “This claim is baseless. You will not find any country that calls for coherence and order in decision-making as much as Iran does. The Americans are well aware of who their counterpart in Iran is and understand how decisions are made there. The problem, in fact, lies in the incoherent statements made by US officials. Highly contradictory stances and frequent shifts in demands and positions constitute the fundamental issue—a point raised not only by us but also by other nations.”

articles.title: US claims it ‘kicked out’ Iranian diplomats
articles.body:
US claims it ‘kicked out’ Iranian diplomats
The US has expelled two more members of the Iranian delegation that attended the UN General Assembly in New York after they allegedly ignored an order to leave the country, AFP and Axios reported on Saturday, citing a State Department official.
US and Iranian negotiators separately met with mediators last month without reaching a breakthrough, leaving the Middle East bracing for a potential resumption of hostilities. US media reported that after the sides failed to reach an agreement on Monday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio ordered Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and other diplomats to leave the country earlier than planned.
“Two more members of the Iranian delegation were found still in [New York] long after the United Nations General Assembly had passed. They have now been kicked out of the US,” a US official told AFP, adding that Rubio “means business.”
According to Axios, one diplomat left on Friday night and the other on Saturday morning.
The Iranian mission to the UN previously disputed Washington’s account of the delegation’s departure, saying its members left in accordance with a schedule communicated to the US before the General Assembly session.
“Having achieved nothing, the State Department has resorted to propagating baseless and worthless news,” the mission wrote on X on Thursday.
US President Donald Trump has resumed threats to “annihilate” Iran’s leadership in recent weeks, hinting that he could order new strikes unless Tehran accepts his terms.
Iranian officials and the military say they are prepared for further escalation.
“After one failure after another, the worst president in American history just keeps talking – and talking – and now his words have even outrun his own fantasies. You can win every day in your own imagination. But reality is shaped by Iran – by its people, its soldiers, and its missiles,” Mohsen Rezaei, the head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, wrote on X on Friday.
The standoff comes as the US reinforces its military presence in the Middle East. The USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group and USS Makin Island amphibious ready group are heading to the region, adding 9,000 to 10,000 sailors and Marines.
The USS George Washington and USS George H.W. Bush are already operating there. If both remain when the Theodore Roosevelt arrives, the US could have three aircraft carriers in the Middle East by late October.
Some US officials reportedly believe Trump could resume major combat operations after the midterm elections in early November. The war remains unpopular among Americans, with 71% of registered voters saying the Trump administration lacks a clear strategy for ending the conflict, according to a recent Fox News poll.

articles.title: The G7 Is Releasing Emergency Fuel Reserves. How Much Will It Help Americans?
articles.body:
The Group of Seven (G7) countries said Friday that the nations would release 100 million barrels of oil and fuel products in the coming months, starting with “substantial” amounts of diesel. The move comes amid a global shortage largely attributed to slowdowns of the passage of oil through the Strait of Hormuz.
A joint statement from the G7 nations—Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom, and the U.S.—confirmed that the International Energy Agency (IEA) will coordinate the release over the next four months.
It calls the move a part of “decisive, coordinated measures to stabilize immediate energy supplies” amid record-high fuel prices driven by the war in Iran and the recent escalation of fighting between Russia and Ukraine.
Read More: Once Again, Energy Is Power
“Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil,” President Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social on Friday. “The process will begin immediately.”
In talks leading up to the announcement on Friday, Trump had been pushing European partners for the release, citing high fuel prices for Americans. Last month, the Trump Administration threatened to temporarily suspend its exports of diesel—earning immediate backlash from countries that rely on it, including Canada, Mexico, and much of Europe.
European leaders and oil executives at the time said that such a ban would be disastrous for long-term oil flow. For that reason, experts believe the threat helped pressure those nations to release their fuel reserves.
The agreement could offer some relief for Americans even if the released diesel stays in Europe, because Europe buys some of its diesel from the U.S. Releasing European reserves could ease competition for U.S. diesel and potentially reduce prices for American buyers.
This is especially critical as the cost of Brent crude oil sits at $102 per barrel as of Oct. 3 and on-highway diesel hit a high of $6.529 per gallon as of last month, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.
But how much relief consumers will actually see—and how quickly—will depend on what type of fuel is released, how much reaches the market and when, and whether supply disruptions persist.
What is actually being added to the market?
Although the G7 shared how much fuel it would release, it did not specify the full breakdown of the release by fuel type. Its statement did say, however, that there will be a “frontloaded” and substantial release of diesel fuel within the first 20 days.
While crude oil must be refined into products like gasoline before consumers can use it, diesel is already a finished fuel. That means a diesel release could address the immediate shortage more directly.
The planned release could help ease shortages of both crude oil and refined fuels, with supplies disrupted by the wars in Iran and Ukraine.
The supply of crude oil has been heavily disrupted this year after the U.S. and Israel launched joint strikes that ignited a war with Iran in February. In response, Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in March. More recent negotiations to end the war have largely failed to address differing opinions on ownership and control over the Strait. This has critically restricted the passage of oil-carrying vessels through the waterway, with daily shipping traffic in the single digits last month, down from pre-war averages of roughly 138 to 140 daily transits.
Diesel, meanwhile, is essential to U.S. transportation, agriculture, and manufacturing: Most goods, food, and manufacturing supplies across the country are transported by heavy-duty trucks and trains running on diesel engines. The war in Iran has driven diesel prices up and lowered supply, but Russia and Ukraine’s targeting of one another’s energy infrastructure has further exacerbated the issue.
While the U.S. in particular does not heavily rely on Russian diesel, America is vulnerable to the volatility caused by Russia removing it from the global market. Trump has claimed outright that Ukraine’s targeting of Russian oil infrastructure is to blame for diesel shortages.
What could Americans feel, and when?
Jason Bordoff, founding director of the Center on Global Energy Policy at Columbia University, says it’s difficult to predict the consumer impact given the scarce details shared so far.
“It makes a big difference if the release is in the next two weeks or if it's four months from now,” Bordoff says.
“I think if we saw some announcement tomorrow from Germany or France that gave concrete, specific numbers for a substantial amount—50 million barrels or so—of diesel, then it could have a real impact if this release actually happens in a timely fashion,” Bordoff says.
At the same time, Jeff Colgan, a professor of political science at Brown University, cautions that American consumers may see limited benefits.
“Releasing diesel could make a difference on price, especially in tight markets in Europe,” Colgan says. “But American consumers are unlikely to see much of a price drop from this policy move unless the diesel share of that 100 million barrels is very large.”
With a timely release of diesel, Bordoff predicts that Americans could see a drop by as much as 25 cents per gallon after a few weeks—but, he adds, the markets seem pretty unsure that that will actually happen.
And market perception is central to whether or not prices drop in the short term.
“I think they’re saying: Show me the barrels, so I have confidence this is real, and it's going to happen quickly,” he says.
David Bieri, an economist and associate professor of urban affairs and planning at Virginia Tech, tells TIME that international interventions like this help “signal” to markets that governments are a credible safety net in prolonged periods of uncertainty.
“That's the main mechanism, because they want to influence market sentiment,” Bieri says. “Then, futures markets begin to price more optimistically, and then eventually the hope is that prices will come down.”
The effect Bieri is describing has already begun: The price of diesel futures in the United States fell 8% on Friday morning, a sign of more optimism in the market.
Bordoff adds that they are also, in part, a response to Trump dropping his threat of a diesel export ban—a threat that was lifted as a condition of the G7 agreement.
The release itself may not impact the markets “an awful lot,” Bieri says, given the broader context of the war with Iran.
“In fact, consumers might not necessarily notice it, ever. That's how insignificant the quantity itself is,” he says of the 100 million barrels. “But it's the importance of the cooperative signal that hopefully will make things better this fall.”
Bieri also cautions that any savings could take time to reach consumers, as carriers and other distributors may use lower fuel costs to rebuild their margins.
“[They] have been bleeding on increased fuel costs,” he says. “This is going to be, if anything, a welcome reprieve for their profit margins, and they're not going to pass that on immediately to consumers.”
What happens if the supply gap is still there when releases taper off?
This October announcement is not the first of its kind: Following the initial market shock of the war in Iran, IEA member countries announced a 400-million-barrel release in March—80% of which has already been released. Notably, the latest announcement did not clearly establish how much of the forthcoming release would be additional to earlier commitments.
In March, the IEA said that the majority of the barrel release would be crude oil; however, reports show that Europe has primarily contributed refined oil, like diesel—which could suggest more of the same in this latest round.
In either event, such fuel releases are just a matter of sticking a bandage over the larger issue of two unresolved wars and continued global energy disruption, says Bordoff.
“We're going to continue to have oil, gasoline, and diesel price shocks until that conflict comes to some sort of resolution, and energy flows can get going again,” he says. “Inventories, and stocks and other schemes like waiving state fuel taxes or something can help on the margin for temporary disruptions, but at some point this isn't temporary anymore.”
Michael Noel, economist at Texas Tech University, agrees with Bordoff, telling TIME that “unless something dramatic happens to end the Ukraine and Iran conflicts, the supply shortage will persist.”
Negotiations between Iranian leadership and the Trump Administration have stalled multiple times in the last six months. Trump said on Sept. 9 that he expected a resolution to come after the midterm elections, which take place in the U.S. on Nov. 3.
“I think the war's going to end immediately after the election because they can't hold out any longer,” he said last month. “Right after the election, oil prices are going to be tumbling downward.”
Axios reported, however, that senior Trump Administration officials met at Camp David to discuss the war on Friday. The talks come as the U.S. last week added economic pressure in the region with a series of sanctions aiming to curtail funding streams and stymy industrial lifelines for Iran.
Experts argue that the fuel crisis and volatility exposes the need for the U.S. to adapt to a changing energy ecosystem. Notably, Colgan says that would include “the national security advantages of clean technologies like EVs, batteries, and renewable energy.”

articles.title: ‘Everyone knows’ Kiev is embezzling Western aid – ex-Polish PM
articles.body:
‘Everyone knows’ Kiev is embezzling Western aid – ex-Polish PM
Ukrainian officials are embezzling foreign financial aid, former Polish Prime Minister Leszek Miller has said, adding that Kiev’s backers are well aware of the corruption but prefer not to ask questions.
Speaking on the ‘Jankowski Kontra’ podcast on Polsat News on Saturday, Miller called for suspending aid to Ukraine until Kiev accounts for previously supplied weapons and funds.
“Nobody’s asking what happened to the 300 tanks we sent in the first phase. What happened to the heavy equipment, the lighter equipment... Nobody’s asking what happened to the billions of euros we donated. Mr. Zelensky simply comes and says, ‘Give it’, and we give it,” Miller stated.
Asked whether he suspected that funds transferred to Ukraine were being embezzled, Miller replied: “Of course, everyone knows it.”The veteran politician argued that Warsaw should demand an accounting of how its assistance has been used and halt further support if Kiev fails to provide one.
“This is a fundamental issue: I’ll lend you the money, but give me a report on what you did with the previous installment,” Miller stated. “Without that help, there is no Ukraine… But we are not a country that is overflowing with wealth… We have obligations to our own citizens, and we cannot simply throw away money and equipment indiscriminately.”
Poland has been one of Kiev’s staunchest backers in its conflict with Russia, pouring billions into military, financial and humanitarian aid while serving as a crucial hub for Western supplies. Yet relations have increasingly soured over Kiev’s honoring of Ukrainian Nazi collaborators linked to the World War II-era Volhynia massacres, in which UPA militants, linked to the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN), killed at least 100,000 ethnic Poles.
Warsaw recognizes the killings as genocide, while Kiev honors figures including OUN leader Stepan Bandera. Tensions flared again this year after Zelensky bestowed the title ‘Heroes of the UPA’ on the Ukrainian Special Operations Center North military unit. In the aftermath, Polish President Karol Nawrocki stripped him of the country’s highest honor, politicians on both sides renounced state decorations, and Warsaw threatened to obstruct Ukraine’s EU accession.
Relations have also been strained by mounting opposition to Ukrainian refugees. A July CBOS survey found that 52% of Poles now opposed accepting them, against 42% in favor – a sharp reversal from the overwhelming support seen after Kiev’s conflict with Moscow escalated in 2022. Tensions deepened earlier this month after a 31-year-old Ukrainian man stabbed five people at a Benedictine abbey in Jaroslaw, killing a priest.
Poland is also not alone in questioning funding for Kiev. Despite receiving billions in Western assistance over the past four years, Ukraine faces a severe cash squeeze and has been pressing European backers for more money. But a string of high-level graft scandals has heightened scrutiny in Brussels, the largest of which centers on an alleged $100 million kickback scheme at state nuclear operator Energoatom, which was reportedly led by Timur Mindich, a former business partner of Vladimir Zelensky.
Western-backed investigators have uncovered multiple other graft schemes involving Ukrainian officials, including one reported earlier this month in which they allegedly embezzled more than $3 million through the delivery of used Soviet-made metro cars donated by Poland.
Against that backdrop, the EU this week rebuffed Kiev’s bid to fast-track its latest €90 billion support loan, making clear that further funds depend on Ukraine delivering promised anti-corruption and governance reforms.

articles.title: North Korea launches ballistic missile over 700 kilometers as hostilities heat up
articles.body:
North Korea fired a ballistic missile toward the sea off its east coast on Saturday, South Korea and Japan said, its latest missile launch this year, which came a day after it rejected Seoul's accusation that its mines wounded soldiers.
The missile was launched from the Wonsan area at around 6:30 a.m. on Saturday and flew more than 700 kilometers (434 miles), the South Korean military said in a statement. Seoul and Washington were analyzing the test for details, it added.
Japan's coast guard, in an emailed statement citing the Japanese defense ministry, said the object may have been a ballistic missile and appeared to have come down, warning ships to take precautions.
South Korea's military said it has raised its monitoring of any further missile tests and will share intelligence with the US and Japan.
The South Korean presidential office's national security council convened an emergency meeting on Saturday to assess the situation after the missile launch, the office said in a statement.
North Korea tested missiles at least 10 times this year, ramps up hostility
North Korea has launched missile tests on more than 10 occasions so far this year. Pyongyang has sometimes said it was testing new types of weapons systems. Some of the tests have come after North Korea protested joint military drills between Seoul and Washington.
The launch came after Pyongyang's Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of leader Kim Jong Un, issued a statement on Friday that dismissed Seoul's demand for an apology for what it said were North Korean mines that seriously wounded South Korean soldiers in the Demilitarised Zone, a heavily fortified area between the two Koreas.
South Korea said this week that North Korean mines caused the blast that seriously injured two South Korean soldiers on a reconnaissance mission inside the 4-km-wide (2.5-mile) border that stretches across the Korean Peninsula.
The missile test may be an attempt by Pyongyang to draw a response from South Korea to the sister's statement, said Cheong Seong-chang, vice president at the Sejong Institute in Seoul, a research center on North Korean affairs. North Korea may also have tested a new type of missile, he added.
North Korea has sharply ramped up hostility against the South in recent years, disavowing unification as a national goal and calling South Korea its "primary foe."

articles.title: Trump says Iran has 'virtually given up' any plans for nuclear weapons
articles.body:
Ahmet Salih Alacaci
04 October 2026•Update: 04 October 2026
US President Donald Trump suggested on Saturday that Iran has “virtually given up” any plans to develop nuclear weapons, one of his administration’s most frequently stated objectives in the war with Tehran, now in its eighth month.
Trump also claimed oil prices were currently decreasing, long elevated after Israel and the US launched strikes against Iran on Feb. 28.
“Oil is coming down. Oil is right now lower, and it's been lower than it was under the Biden administration, and they did nothing about the fact that Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon,” Trump told reporters as he departed the White House to attend a rally in the state of Ohio.
“By the way, Iran, as you know, has virtually given up any plans of a nuclear weapon,” he added.
Iran has long denied accusations by the US and Israel that it seeks to develop nuclear weapons, a position reiterated by President Masoud Pezeshkian during his visit last month to New York for the UN General Assembly.
Pezeshkian said Tehran is not seeking nuclear weapons because of a religious prohibition, and offered to dilute its enriched uranium stockpiles under international verification.
Iran, however, has maintained that it will not compromise on its peaceful civilian nuclear program or make structural concessions unless the US lifts economic sanctions.

articles.title: Drones Attack Khanskaya Military Airbase in Russia’s Adygea Region
articles.body:
Strike drones attacked the Khanskaya military airbase in Russia’s Republic of Adygea during the night of October 4, 2026.
Footage published by the Exilenova+ outlet appears to show the attack.
The military airbase is located about 6 km northwest of Maykop and 3 km east of the village of Khanskaya.
Reports of a drone threat began coming in at 1:42 a.m. and continued until 5:34 a.m.
During this time, Russian monitoring channels reported detecting drones and active air defense operations in the region and around the airbase.
NASA FIRMS data from geostationary satellites also confirmed a fire in the area of the military airbase.
Russian military aviation currently uses the airbase. It is located at coordinates 44°40′47″N, 40°02′00″E. The site is approximately 500 km from Ukrainian-controlled territory.
Historically, the airbase hosted military aviation training units, including the 761st Training Aviation Regiment. After the regiment was disbanded in 2009, the 272nd Training Aviation Base was established.
Military Unit 55661 is part of the A. K. Serov Krasnodar Higher Military Aviation School for Pilots.
Despite the presence of training aviation units, the airbase has previously been targeted by Ukrainian strikes.
On October 10, 2024, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported that Su-34, Su-27, and Su-35 aircraft were based at the airfield and were being used by Russian aviation in the war against Ukraine.
Militarnyi previously reported that drones attacked the airbase on December 25, 2025. Another attack took place on December 29 of the same year.

articles.title: Trump says Iran dropped nuclear weapon plans
articles.body:
AA Photo
US President Donald Trump said on Oct. 3 Iran has virtually abandoned its drive to develop nuclear weapons because severe financial exhaustion and regional setbacks crippled Tehran's strategic leverage.
Speaking to reporters, Trump said Iranian authorities no longer possess the capability or ambition to produce an atomic bomb and are eager to negotiate a new settlement. "They have virtually given up any plans for nuclear weapons," he said.
Trump reiterated his position an Iranian nuclear weapon remains unacceptable, asserting earlier maximum pressure sanctions and subsequent economic isolation had drained Tehran's revenue before recent regional conflicts further weakened the government.
The remarks come as international observers continue to monitor Tehran's atomic program. The International Atomic Energy Agency reported earlier this year Iran had accumulated an enriched uranium stockpile with purity levels reaching 60 percent, just below the 90 percent threshold required for weapons-grade material.
Tehran has consistently maintained its atomic work remains exclusively civilian, focused on energy generation and medical research. The diplomatic dispute intensified in 2018 when the US unilaterally pulled out of the 2015 nuclear accord, formally known as the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, before reimposing sweeping banking and oil sanctions on the Islamic republic.

articles.title: Latvia's pro-Ukraine party wins parliamentary election by wide margin
articles.body:
Latvia's ruling party, the centrist, pro-Ukrainian United List faction led by Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs, has won the country's parliamentary election with over 35% of the vote.
Nearly 800,000 Latvians took to the polls on Oct. 3, representing a turnout of 51.8%, according to the Central Election Commission. United List won 35.3% of the vote, earning them 41 seats in the Saeima, Latvia's 100-member unicameral parliament.
"I congratulate Andris Kulbergs on his convincing victory in the parliamentary elections in Latvia," President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on X on Oct. 4.
"This strong result reflects the Latvian people's confidence in your leadership and your vision for the country's future. Ukraine deeply appreciates Latvia's unwavering friendship and support."
Latvians took to the polls on Oct. 3 to decide what their parliament will look like for the next four years. Affordability and security concerns have been top political issues in the Baltic country which shares a border with Russia and is home to a large Russian-speaking minority.
The election marked a test for Kulbergs, who has been prime minister since May, following a political crisis triggered by a Ukrainian drone incursion into Latvian airspace. Former Prim Minister Evika Silina was forced to resign, leading to a government collapse that paved the way for a four-party coalition led by Kulbergs.
Affordability and security concerns were the top political issues for Latvians going into the Oct. 3 vote. Warnings from Western officials over escalating hybrid threats from Russia are taken seriously by the Baltic nation, an EU and NATO member which shares a border with both Russia and Belarus.
The populist Latvia First party came second in the parliamentary election, winning about 13%, or 17 seats. The pro-Russian Sovereign Power party ranked third, with 11.7% (15 seats).
Sovereign Power is Latvia's only political party that opposes military aid to Ukraine.
Latvia's conservative National Alliance party came in fourth with 8.9% (10 seats). In fifth place, the Progressive party gained 7.9%, also earning 10 seats.
While pro-Russian parties increased their representation in Latvia's legislature, they still lack the necessary numbers to meaningfully influence policy.
Throughout his term, Kulbergs has expressed unwavering support for Ukraine throughout his term. Latvia has also sharply increased defense spending since 2022, reaching 5% of GDP — one of the highest levels in NATO.

articles.title: EU responds to Russian threats against European diplomats in Kyiv
articles.body:
EU responds to Russian threats against European diplomats in Kyiv
European Commission spokesman Christian Wigand has said that, despite Russia's threats of massive attacks against foreign diplomats and embassies remaining in Kyiv, the EU delegation will continue to work in the Ukrainian capital, and that Russia will not intimidate Europe or force it to stop supporting Ukraine.
Source: Ukrinform and Ukrainian public broadcaster hromadske, citing Wigand's comments
Details: Wigand said this was not the first time Russia had resorted to such threats, which he said shows that the Kremlin is losing its war and losing its nerve. The spokesman noted that Moscow is trying to intimidate Europe into scaling back its support for Ukraine, adding that this will not happen, and that the EU will continue to support Ukraine, expose Russia's irresponsible and dangerous actions, and keep increasing pressure on it.
The European Commission spokesman was responding to a statement by Russia's Foreign Ministry on 3 October, in which Russia once again called on foreign citizens and diplomats to leave Kyiv and refrain from visiting Ukraine.
Russia said it will continue carrying out massive strikes on Ukrainian cities, including the capital, and claimed that those who ignore the warning will themselves be responsible for any negative consequences and will be "knowingly putting their lives in mortal danger".
Wigand, however, said that the EU's diplomatic mission in Kyiv remains operational.
The spokesman said the EU is currently preparing the largest sanctions package against Russia in its history, and had already introduced new restrictions this week in response to the deportation of Ukrainian children.
He cited EU High Representative Kaja Kallas as saying that Russia is prepared to take greater risks, but noted that the EU is also stepping up its own actions to make Russia pay an even higher price.
Separately, Wigand stressed the increase in volumes of military aid to Kyiv. In particular, the EU has approved plans for defence procurement for Ukraine worth €28.3 billion for this year and is allocating an additional €6.6 billion directly for military aid.
Background:
- Ahead of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, a number of European countries evacuated their embassies from Kyiv to Lviv and Poland.
- On 2 October, The Guardian reported that, amid intensifying Russian attacks, some Western embassies are drawing up contingency plans for evacuation to Lviv or eastern Poland, despite public statements about their intention to remain in the Ukrainian capital.
- Foreign Ministry spokesman Heorhii Tykhyi later said that foreign partners had not informed Ukraine of any intentions to relocate their diplomatic missions from Kyiv.

articles.title: Russia's Defense Ministry said it would intensify strikes on Ukraine's "military facilities"
articles.body:
Russia's Defense Ministry said it would intensify strikes on Ukraine's "military facilities"
Kyiv • UNN
Russia's Defense Ministry announced that it would intensify strikes on Ukraine's military facilities. The purported reason was Zelenskyy's statement about responding with strikes on Russian oil refineries.
Russia will intensify strikes on military and military-industrial facilities in Kyiv and other regions of Ukraine following Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's statement about increasing attacks on Russian oil refineries. This is stated in a statement by Russia's Defense Ministry, UNN reports.
Following Zelenskyy's statement today, strikes by the armed forces of the Russian Federation on military and military-industrial facilities, as well as related infrastructure in Kyiv and other regions of Ukraine, will be intensified
In addition
The day before, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told Reuters in an interview that, according to information he had received, Russia's leadership had lifted restrictions on its military regarding strikes on civilian facilities in Ukrainian cities, and that in response Ukraine would intensify strikes on Russian oil refineries.
According to Zelenskyy, Ukrainian intelligence obtained documents indicating that Vladimir Putin had approved a "new doctrine" of strikes against an expanded list of civilian targets in Ukraine ahead of winter.
"We saw the documents and we know that they allowed them (the military) to attack infrastructure, logistics, roads, schools, hospitals, in order to force people to leave the capital and various cities. That is the purpose of this operation," Reuters quotes Zelenskyy as saying.

articles.title: In the United States, there is renewed talk of redeploying U.S. troops from Europe: Europeans are to ensure the continent’s defense – Hegseth
articles.body:
In the United States, there is renewed talk of redeploying U.S. troops from Europe: Europeans are to ensure the continent’s defense – Hegseth
Kyiv • UNN
The Pentagon is reviewing the U.S. military presence in Europe. Some forces may be moved to the Western Hemisphere to combat drug cartels.
U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said that some of the American military forces and capabilities currently stationed in Europe could be redeployed to the Western Hemisphere. Washington plans to strengthen its military presence in Central and South America amid the fight against drug cartels, The Hill reports, writes UNN.
Details
According to Hegseth, the new U.S. strategy envisages greater "burden-sharing" in Europe, meaning that NATO allies should take on more responsibility for the continent’s conventional defense.
Some of these capabilities will be moved elsewhere, either back home (...) or to another position in the Western Hemisphere, as we fight these designated terrorist organizations
The Pentagon is reviewing its presence in Europe
The Pentagon is currently conducting a six-month review of the U.S. military presence in Europe. Its goal is to determine what share of responsibility for the continent’s defense can be transferred to European NATO allies. The review is expected to be completed in December.
NATO strengthens intelligence sharing due to the threat from Russia24.09.26, 19:39 • 26242 views
At the same time, the United States is expanding defense cooperation with Latin American countries. Hegseth named Ecuador, Honduras, Guatemala, and Panama among its partners.
At the same time, the secretary did not specify how many U.S. troops or which units could leave Europe. No final decisions on the scale of a possible redeployment have been announced yet.

articles.title: USS George H.W. Bush anchors in Thailand for recreational visit after Middle East deployment
articles.body:
The US aircraft carrier George H.W. Bush arrived off Thailand's resort island of Phuket on Sunday with about 4,800 personnel aboard for a rest-and-recreation break after months of supporting US operations in the Middle East.
The Nimitz-class carrier had been operating in the Arabian Sea during the conflict with Iran, according to multiple media reports.
The carrier will anchor offshore, while crew members are expected to come ashore through Phuket Deep Sea Port and spend time on the popular southern resort island from October 4 to 9, local media reported.
A local mayor had estimated that each US service member from the Lincoln could spend up to 3,000 baht ($89) per day during the visit. Thailand is the United States' only treaty partner in mainland Southeast Asia.
The visit follows a five-day port call by the USS Abraham Lincoln at Laem Chabang in eastern Thailand last month, with about 5,000 sailors and Marines aboard.
US carrier Abraham Lincoln departs Thailand after respite visit
The nuclear-powered Lincoln was involved in the US naval blockade and combat operations in the war with Iran and, according to Democratic lawmakers, set a modern-day record for consecutive days at sea.
“We would like to thank the people of Thailand for their incredible hospitality,” US Navy Captain Dan Keeler, the Abraham Lincoln’s commanding officer, said in a statement after the carrier departed in early September.
Busloads of sailors and Marines wearing civilian clothes, many smiling and waving, started arriving at a hotel in the resort city of Pattaya, about 150 km (93 miles) southeast of Bangkok, shortly after their ships docked.
